	- Incorrect behavior: "a folder handed down is never written down" fails, and the test keeps its run folder. The check calls `fTestDir_Record` in the test's own process, which made and owns its folder when nothing was handed down.
	- Expected behavior: The test passes alone as it does under `cleanup/run.bash`, which always hands it a folder.
	- Reproduced: Yes, on b23 and b29w. With `SILKTERM_TEST_DIR` set it passed on b23, and 3 of 3 on b29w.
	- Actual cause: The test checked a handed-down folder in its own process. Run alone, that process made its own folder, so `fTestDir_Record` wrote it down as it should.
	- Actual fix: That check runs in a child with `SILKTERM_TEST_DIR` set, like the check beside it for a folder a run made. It also checks the handed-down folder is never removed.
	- Verified: 20261026. Alone, it failed before the fix and passed after, 3 of 3 here and 3 of 3 on b29w, without a run folder left in the temp folder. It still passes with `SILKTERM_TEST_DIR` set, and under `cleanup/run.bash`. With the guard in `fTestDir_Record` taken out, the new check failed. `--backlog-run-quick scripts` passed.
	- Swept: the other checks in `win.ps1`, and `testdir/remove.ps1`. No other check reads the process's own folder state as a handed-down one.
	- Test case: de5ea, `cicd/tests/cleanup/win.ps1`.
	- Branch: rnd1026
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: a test-only fix whose test passes alone and in the suite.
	- Closed: 20261026-172644

- A config test's 50 ms bound for a failed write went red under load in a full run
	- ID: 2026102410441001
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261024-104410
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026102407430379
	- Target OS: Linux
	- Test environment: b23 at load about 20 to 30, the full run in the container at 550ff60 on `rnd1024`
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run the full run while the box is busy.
	- Incorrect behavior: `config::tests::a_failed_write_that_left_the_file_changes_nothing` failed its "no pause when the file is still there" check, under 50 ms, in the testdir step's read-only run (ddazx). The full run stopped in stage 3 there.
	- Expected behavior: A timing bound doesn't go red on load alone.
	- Reproduced: No. Run alone 3 times right after, at load 23, it passed each time.
		- 20261025: Yes, inside a 5% CPU quota beside 2 busy loops: 4 of 40 runs failed, each at about 98.5 ms.
	- Actual cause: It was a wall clock bound. Under a CPU quota, which is how a container's `--cpus` works, the whole group stalls for the rest of a 100 ms period once it uses up its share, so a bound under 100 ms can fail on load alone. The write itself doesn't pause there.
	- Actual fix: The restore counts its pauses on the test's thread, and the test checks the count is 0 instead of timing the write. The sibling `a_restore_that_cannot_write_gives_up_and_says_so` (dcfxc) checks 5 pauses in place of its under-2 s bound, and keeps its at-least-400 ms bound, which load can't fail.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261025: The Miri ignore on this test is gone, since it had only failed the time bound there.
	- Verified: 20261025. Under the same quota the fixed test passed 40 of 40, and dcfxc 15 of 15. With a pause put before the name check, the test failed on the count. Under Miri, it, dcfxc and `a_restore_never_writes_through_a_name_taken_meanwhile` pass. The 232 config tests, fmt, and clippy for Linux and Windows with all targets pass.
	- Swept: every wall clock bound in the unit tests. The rest have 0.9 s or more of slack (peers, term, shells). The 2 Windows restore tests (dcfz9, dcfza) are left as they were, since dcfza's 1400 ms bound is part of its race with a 1500 ms hold.
	- Branch: rnd1025
	- Test case: `a_failed_write_that_left_the_file_changes_nothing` (dcfxa), same ID, rewritten in place. It was red under the quota before, and green after.
	- Closed: 20261025-065046

- The allocations per frame test failed its drag limit once under load
	- ID: 2026102321230038
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: ddkre passed in the gate step's container run at 550ff60, with the box at load about 20.
	- Closed: 20261024-104410
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261023-212300
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026102407065855, 2026102407065861
	- Target OS: Linux
	- Test environment: b23 at load 23 to 25, the quick gate in the container on `rnd1023`, llvmpipe
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run `cicd/cicd.bash -y --quick --no-publish --no-dogfood --no-demo` while the box is busy.
	- Incorrect behavior: `cicd/tests/allocs/run.bash` (ddkre) failed with "drag: 364 per frame, limit 360". The same binary then passed 3 times in a row, at 339, 346, and 347.
	- Expected behavior: The drag check doesn't go red on load alone.
	- Reproduced: 20261023, once in 4 runs. Gate log `/mnt/ext/wip2/wip/tmp/silkterm-floss/20261023-211203/001/gate.log`.
		- 20261024: on b23 with 8 cores loaded, the old drag failed 2 runs in 3, at 362 and 368, and read 350 on the third.
	- Possible cause: The test's own comment says the per-frame count in a drag rises with load, since a slow box folds more moves into each frame. The frame's own count still drifts with it, and 360 leaves about 4% over the measured 340.
	- Actual cause:
		- The drag frame had 2 shares that grow with load. Measured per frame on the debug build:
			- The minimap recomposes once its 90 ms gap is up, about 20 allocations. An idle box composes on every third drag frame or so, a busy one on every frame. With the map off, a one-row drag read a flat 320.
			- Each row the selection newly spans costs about 17. At 80 frames for 80 moves a frame spans a third of a row. At 13 frames each spans 2 or more, which read 359 to 370.
		- The first has a ceiling, one compose a frame. The second doesn't.
	- Actual fix:
		- The drag goes down to select the rows first, waits a second for that frame, and only then is counted, moving along that one row. A busy box can then add no more than the compose. The limit stays 360.
		- The at-rest check at load 50 (2026102407065855) and the drag's needless minimap compose (2026102407065861) were filed separately.
	- Verified: 20261024, the new drag check passed 6 runs at load 30 to 52, at 336, 339, and 345 with no extra load, adn 335, 335, and 331 with 8 cores loaded. The old one, alternated with it under that load, failed 2 of 3.
		- At load 52 both versions failed the at-rest check instead, which is 2026102407065855.
		- shellcheck is clean.
	- Swept: the at-rest and per-move checks in the same test, and every reader of the allocation counter. No other test reads it.
	- Branch: rnd1024
	- Test case: ddkre itself. The old drag failing under load and the new one passing are under Verified.

- The allocations per frame test fails its at-rest limit at load 50 or so, with the shells' output still coming in
	- ID: 2026102407065855
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: ddkre passed in the gate step's container run at 550ff60, with the box at load about 20.
	- Closed: 20261024-104410
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261024-070658
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026102321230038, 2026102407065861
	- Target OS: Linux
	- Test environment: b23 at load 42 to 52, with 8 cores also loaded, llvmpipe
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run `cicd/tests/allocs/run.bash` (ddkre) on a box at load 50 or so.
	- Incorrect behavior: "at rest: 15552 per frame, limit 178", and 3914 on the next run. The old and the new drag both failed it the same way.
	- Expected behavior: The at-rest check counts frames at rest, at any load.
	- Reproduced: 20261024, 2 runs in a row at load 52. At load 30 to 42 it passed 6 times.
		- 20261024: again with the test and 24 busy loops on the same 8 cores, at 13511, 15852, 3073, and 634.
	- Possible cause: The test waits 6 s after the window is up before it counts. At that load the 3 shells' 400 colored lines each are still being drawn, so the window isn't at rest yet. The drag check can also see as few as 9 frames there, against its floor of 6.
	- Actual cause:
		- There were 2 launch steps still going 6 s after the window was up:
			- The shells' output was still easing in, at 1 or 2 frames a second, up to about 20 s after launch.
			- The shell scan starts 3 s after the window shows. Under load it came back later, and folding it in, which rewrites the config, made about 87000 allocations between 2 frames.
		- Either one in the counted 4 s fails the check. The scan alone did it in runs where the output had already settled.
	- Actual fix:
		- `SILK_ALLOCS` now ends each frame's line with what it was drawn for (`for cursor`, `for rebuild+scroll+cursor` and so on), and prints a line when the shell scan is folded in.
		- The test waits, up to 60 s, for that line and then 5 frames in a row drawn for the cursor alone. It counts until it has 20 frames or 20 s have passed, at least 4 s. A window that never comes to rest fails a check of its own.
	- Verified: 20261024, with the test and 24 busy loops on the same 8 cores, box load 12 to 72. The new at-rest check passed 10 runs in a row, at 170 to 173. The old count, alternated with it on the same build, failed 3 of 3. With no extra load it passed at 167.
		- `a_frame_cause_prints_the_words_the_window_test_reads` (dec7m) passes. Unit suite, clippy for Linux and Windows, fmt, shellcheck, and the test ID check pass.
	- Swept: every reader of the `[allocs]` lines. Only ddkre reads them, and its drag count reads the new line format too. The drag starts after the count at rest, so it waits for rest as well.
	- Branch: rnd1024
	- Test case: ddkre itself, and dec7m for the words it reads. The old count failing under load and the new one passing are under Verified.

- The nightly warns that silkterm's `Send` check on wgpu's types passes the recursion limit, which a later Rust makes an error
	- ID: 2026102321073303
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261023-210733
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026102320591313
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Build the tests on nightly-2026-10-16, as the Miri run does.
	- Incorrect behavior:
		- A `recursion_depth_exceeding_limit` warning on the whole crate, from proving `wgpu_core`'s `Global` is `Send`. It says it's being phased out to a hard error, rust-lang/rust#159228.
	- Expected behavior:
		- No warning, so a toolchain bump past the change still builds.
	- Possible cause:
		- The default limit of 128. The warning suggests `#![recursion_limit = "256"]`, or a manual `Send` impl on a type in between.
	- Reproduced: 20261024 on b23. nightly-2026-10-16 warns once, at the dialog GPU warm-up thread in `gfx.rs`, for the plain build and the tests, and for the Windows target too. Stable 1.96 says nothing, since it doesn't have that lint.
	- Actual cause:
		- Proving `Option<DialogGpu>` is `Send` walks `wgpu::Queue` down through `wgpu_core`'s `Global`, its registries and storage, past 128 levels. The new trait solver counts that depth where the old one didn't. wgpu is a known case upstream (gfx-rs/wgpu#9608), and rustc plans to fix most of it before the new solver is the default.
	- Actual fix: `#![recursion_limit = "256"]` in `main.rs`. The issue's other way is a manual `unsafe impl Send` on a type in between, which adds unsafe code to quiet a warning. A higher limit only costs a library its users, and this is a binary.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261024: Verified: on nightly-2026-10-16, the workspace with all targets, and the Windows and macOS targets with `-Zbuild-std`, check with no warning. Without the line the Linux and Windows checks warn again. Stable fmt check and clippy for Linux pass. `cicd/utility/gpu-stress` checks clean on the nightly too.
		- 20261024: Not checked on the sanitizer nightly, nightly-2026-10-15, which is only in the image. It's a day older than the one checked.
	- Swept: the other crate roots, knobs and the `glyphon_gl` example, and `cicd/utility/gpu-stress`. None warns.
	- Test case: None. Only a nightly has the lint, and stable doesn't know its name, so a `deny` on it would break the stable build.
	- Branch: rnd1024
	- Closed: 20261024-065132

- The Settings dialog's spec leaks the strings of rows it drops, and each test that parses it leaks a whole copy
	- ID: 2026101912070933
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261019-120709
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026101714445002, 2026101714445005
	- Incorrect behavior: `ui_spec` keeps the strings of `settings_ui.shcl` by leaking them for a `'static` lifetime. The rows that are dropped for the platform, and each tip that's replaced by its warning, leak for good, once per process. Every test that parses the spec leaks all of it.
	- Expected behavior: Nothing the parse made becomes unreachable.
	- Reproduced: 20261019, by the test suite under LSan.
	- Possible cause: `keep` and `keep_all` in ui_spec.rs leak each string, and `keep_platform` and `pick_warnings` then drop some of them.
	- Notes:
		- `cicd/lsan-suppressions.txt` lets `silkterm::ui_spec::` through with this ID beside it. Take that line out with the fix.
		- With the line gone, the test stand-in `stand_in_tabs` in settings_ui.rs shows a leak of its own too, since it builds its tree through ui_spec.
		- The heap-growth test in heap_growth.rs has a `known:` line with this ID too. Take it out with the fix.
	- Actual cause: As the possible cause says. The stand-in also leaked its own copy of the tab tree on every call.
	- Actual fix: `keep` goes through text.rs's `intern`, and `keep_all` keeps one copy of each distinct list the same way. A string a parse drops stays reachable, and a second parse adds nothing. The stand-in keeps one copy per distinct tree. The suppression and the `known:` line are gone, and design.md no longer names the spec as a known growth.
	- Branch: rnd1022
	- Test case: de5j3 (`the_heap_stops_growing_after_a_warm_up`) without its `known:` line, and the ui_spec and stand-in tests under LSan with no suppression.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261022: Verified both ways. The heap-growth test failed before (+454820 bytes over 20 parses) and reads flat after (+0). Under LSan with the suppression gone, the 13 ui_spec tests reported 155223 bytes leaked before and nothing after. The 5 tests that use `stand_in_tabs` reported 6912 bytes from it with only the ui_spec half fixed, and nothing after.
		- The full ASan suite with an empty suppression list is part of 2026101714445002's queued run. Its heap-growth run should now show all 6 actions flat.
	- Swept: every `String::leak`, `Vec::leak`, `Box::leak` and `mem::forget` in source/src. The ones left are text.rs's `intern`, ui_spec's `keep_all` and the stand-in, all reachable from a static, and term.rs's Windows test.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: a mechanical fix, proven failing before and passing after under both dhat and LSan.
	- Closed: 20261022-105400

- On a Mac where `bash` is Apple's 3.2, 4 prompt tests fail
	- ID: 2026102113432601
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261021-134326
	- Opened by: CC
	- Assigned to: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026102113432600
	- Target OS: macOS
	- Test environment: GitHub macos-15, arm64
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run `cargo test` on a Mac without a newer bash ahead of /bin/bash on PATH.
	- Incorrect behavior:
		- These fail with `bash: ${PS1@P}: bad substitution`: `a_pane_prompt_shows_the_git_part_only_inside_a_working_tree`, `a_branch_name_is_shown_and_never_run_by_the_prompt`, `the_prompt_arrow_is_one_a_mac_has_a_font_for`, `the_prompt_shows_any_repository_and_how_far_it_is_from_upstream`.
	- Expected behavior: The tests use a bash that can run them, or skip and say why.
	- Reproduced: 20261021, GitHub macos-15 runner, 2 runs.
	- Possible cause: The tests run `bash` from PATH and expand `${PS1@P}`, which needs bash 4.4. Apple's is 3.2.
	- Notes:
		- `cicd/ci-mac.bash` puts Homebrew's bash first, so the CI run passes.
		- 20261022: The prompt script itself works under bash 3.2.57. It builds the same PS1 as 5.3 outside a repository, inside one, with ahead and behind counts (`↑2↓1`), and on a branch and remote named with `$( )`, backquotes and `${ }`. An interactive 3.2 shell shows those names as text and runs nothing. As root, a `$` in a name shows as `#`, in 5.3 too; the script's own comment already says so.
		- 20261022: Mac CI run 39842974082 on rnd1022, with Homebrew's bash first on PATH. The 4 tests ran and passed, and none were skipped. That run failed on another test, filed on 2026102114411311.
	- Actual cause: The tests ran whatever `bash` was on PATH and expanded `${PS1@P}`, which is bash 4.4.
	- Actual fix: The tests find a bash that can expand `${PS1@P}`: the one on PATH, then Homebrew's in `/opt/homebrew/bin` and `/usr/local/bin`. If there isn't one, each prints "skipped: no bash 4.4 or newer" and returns, which the Mac CI's skips step counts.
	- Verified: With a bash on PATH that fails on `${PS1@P}` as 3.2 does, the old tests failed 4 of 4 and the new ones skip 4 of 4 with the reason. With the real bash 5 they pass. The script was checked under bash 3.2 and 5.3, as above. fmt and clippy pass on the Linux, Windows, and macOS targets.
	- Not verified: The Homebrew fallback on a Mac whose PATH has only Apple's bash.
	- Swept: Every test that runs `bash` in `source/src`. Only these 4 expand `${PS1@P}`. The strace test runs bash 3.2-safe syntax and skips on a Mac anyway.
	- Branch: rnd1022
	- Test case: The same 4 tests: dcnkv, dcryy, ddkjn, ddmm3.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: red before and green after against a bash that fails as 3.2 does, and the script checked under 3.2.
	- Closed: 20261022-110907

- For a moment after a scale change, programs in the window are told a much smaller or larger grid
	- ID: 2026101412311921
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Needs external testing: On Windows and on macOS, a move between 2 monitors at different scales with a program in the window that logs each resize. It's told one new grid, or with `--columns` and `--rows` the same grid, never one about half or twice the size first.
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261014-123119
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100114435600, 2026101412025603
	- Target OS: All
	- Test environment: b23, headless sway, seen on Wayland
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Move a window from a 100% monitor to a 200% one, with something running that redraws on a resize.
	- Incorrect behavior: The program is told a grid about half as wide and tall for a moment, then the right one. From 125% to 150% it was 71 columns for 87.
	- Expected behavior: It's told only the new grid.
	- Reproduced: 20261014, by the random test, in 2 drags from one run of cases.
	- Possible cause: On a scale change the text is laid out again with the new cells but the window's old size in pixels, until the resize that follows arrives.
	- Actual cause: As above. Confirmed on b23 under headless sway with a program that logs each resize: 80x24 went to 51x14 for 5 ms on the way to 150%, and 161x51 on the way back to 100%. The engine's grid was resized each time too, so long lines were rewrapped twice.
	- Notes:
		- The random test allows it by this ID until it's fixed.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261014: Fixed together with 2026101412003308, and its decision applies. See there for what changed per platform.
	- Actual fix: The panes are laid out for the size the window is about to be. That's the size asked for to keep the grid, or else the system's own. On Wayland and macOS the window already reports it during the change, and on Windows and X11 it's the old size scaled by the change.
		- The same thing happened when a monitor's kept font zoom was taken: the new cells were laid out in the old size, then the window was resized. A grid of 89x16 showed on the way from 110x20 to 60x35. It's laid out once, at the new size, now.
		- On X11, winit reports the old size once more right after a scale change, so the moment can still come there. This was read in winit's code and not seen. X11 changes scale only between monitors of different DPI, with no Xft.dpi set.
	- Test case: `cicd/tests/monwl/run.bash` (ddy98). Its shell now writes every size it's told as well as a sample each tenth of a second. A new check fails on any grid well off the ones the steps took, and the new last part checks a size from the command line. Both were seen failing on the old build. The first also failed with the font zoom part of the fix taken back out. `a_scale_change_lays_out_for_the_size_on_its_way` (ddyr1) for the size worked out. The random test's allowance for this item is gone.
	- Verified:
		- On Wayland, with and without a kept size taking over, and with a kept font zoom: one new grid per change, never one well off.
		- Not verified: Windows, macOS, and X11 at a real scale change, which are compiled only.
	- Swept: everything that rebuilds the text and then resizes. The scale change and a kept font zoom were the 2 that did. A font zoom from the keyboard keeps the window's size by design, so its new grid is the real one. The Settings dialog's own scale change keeps its size in DIP.
	- Branch: scalegrid
	- Commit: 22f315d
	- Closed: 20261017-144436

	- ID: 2026101408384489
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261014-083844
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026101407014142
	- Target OS: All
	- Test environment: b29w
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Turn cursor blink off.
		- Run a command that prints nothing for a few seconds.
	- Incorrect behavior: The tab doesn't name it while it runs.
	- Expected behavior: The tab names it.
	- Reproduced: Seen once on b29w with blink off, with a program cmd didn't wait for. Not checked on Linux.
		- 20261014 on b23 and on b29w and vm925w: Confirmed. On Linux a quiet program started 0.05 to 0.8 s after a frame was never named, 5 of 5. On Windows, ping from PowerShell with its output thrown away was never named, 2 of 2 on each box.
	- Possible cause: What a tab says is kept for 250 ms. A frame drawn right before the command starts keeps "nothing running", and without output or blink, a later frame doesn't ask again. This is plausible, from reading the code only.
	- Actual cause: As above. On Windows the child scan's answer was also kept until the terminal next stirred, so even a later frame got "nothing running".

		- New Windows scenario `quiettab`: failed on dev on b29w and vm925w, passes on the branch on both.
		- `cmdgui` and `conmap` pass on both boxes with the same build.
	- Swept: The tab, the window title, and the minimap column all read the one answer, so the one look is enough for all of them. Copy-output's at-prompt answer is the same scan on Windows, and is only fresher.
	- Branch: conload
	- Commit: af9559d
	- Test case: `cicd/tests/quiettab/run.bash` (ddydc) and wingui scenario `quiettab` (ddydp), both seen failing on dev; `a_quiet_command_is_looked_for_again_after_the_last_stir` (ddydg) pins when the looks come.

		- 20261007: One SIGSEGV of the unit test process was also seen at about load 13, and no core was kept. The suite passed 3 runs alone, and the next 2 pipeline runs passed. It wasn't filed separately, since there's nothing to go on yet.
		- 20261007: One run of the whole suite at about load 70 didn't print a result line, which looks like the same crash. Its exit status wasn't kept. Another 9 loaded runs passed.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261007: Reproduced at 47e33e6, at load 13 to 51 with the rest of the suite looping beside it. The old test failed 3 times in 320.
		- 20261007: Linux and macOS pass in the full pipeline at a8c8be6. Windows failed 1 of 2 runs of its unit suite on vm925w, with a median of 1.15 against the 1.10 limit and pairs from 0.88 to 1.57. The rest of that suite passed. It went back to Queued for the Windows wall clock path.
		- 20261009: Windows never used thread CPU time. It timed by wall clock, since GetThreadTimes moves in scheduler ticks of about 15.6 ms and one run is about 40 ms here. So on Windows the test still counted every turn the rest of the suite took on the cores, which is the first cause again. It now counts the thread's own CPU cycles there, with QueryThreadCycleTime. Linux and macOS are as they were. It's waiting on vm925w.
		- 20261009: Wine 10 fails QueryThreadCycleTime, so this test fails at once under Wine. Nothing runs the unit suite under Wine.
		- 20261014: vm925w is off, so the 5 runs went to b29w, against dev, which has had the fix since 5af2c4a. `the_scroll_record_costs_a_full_screen_program_little` passed in all 5, and in 1 more run before them. The control runs on the build before the fix weren't done.
	- Actual cause: the test took the best time of each side separately, at different moments. Under load, one side could get a quiet moment the other never got. The rows cost about 4% here, so there was little room under the 10% limit.
	- Actual cause, Windows, read from the code: the Windows half timed by wall clock, since thread times there move in 15.6 ms ticks. The pairing alone couldn't make up for it.
	- Actual fix: the test now times by the thread's own CPU time, which leaves out time spent waiting for a core. It runs 15 pairs back to back, order swapped each time, and judges the median of the per-pair ratios. The limit stays at 10%. It also checks the kept row is the very row that left rather than a copy, which fails at once without any timing at all.
	- Actual fix, Windows: it uses the thread's CPU cycles from QueryThreadCycleTime, which counts only while the thread runs and isn't tied to the tick. Only ratios are taken, so the cycle rate doesn't matter.

	- Swept, 20261009: every other thread or process time read. `perf.rs` reads GetThreadTimes for the `SILK_PERF` CPU line, over seconds, where a tick doesn't matter.

With the dropped row copied an extra time it failed 60 of 60 under the same load, median 1.29 to 1.35. With the copy put back in place of the swap, the pointer check failed. The whole suite took the same time with either test, 2 runs each. Pane tests, clippy on the Linux, Windows, and macOS targets, fmt, and the test ID check pass.

On Linux the test passed alone, 20 of 20 at load about 20 with 24 busy loops and the suite looping beside it (medians 1.03 to 1.05), and the whole suite passed once under the same load. - Programs that ask for focus reports never get them
	- ID: 2026101315155800
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261013-151558
	- Opened by: CC
	- Assigned to: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026101310563323
	- Target OS: All
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run a program that turns on focus reports (`CSI ? 1004 h`), such as fish 4 at its prompt, vim, or muffer.
		- Click another window, then back.
	- Incorrect behavior: the program gets nothing. The engine notes the mode, but the window's focus change never sends `CSI I` or `CSI O`.
	- Expected behavior: focus in sends `CSI I` and focus out sends `CSI O` while the mode is on, as xterm does.
	- Reproduced: 20261013, by reading the code. Nothing reads the mode outside the minimap, and the window's focus handler doesn't write anything to the shell.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261013: The pane that has the keyboard is the one told. A pane or tab switch sends `CSI O` to the program leaving and `CSI I` to the one coming in, as kitty, wezterm, and tmux with focus-events do. Losing the window sends `CSI O` to that pane only.
		- 20261013: Nothing is sent when a program first turns the mode on, as in xterm.
		- 20261013: A read-only pane doesn't get reports, the same as mouse reports.
	- Actual cause: Nothing sent focus reports. The engine only records the mode.
	- Actual fix:
		- Each pass works out which pane has the keyboard, or none while the window is unfocused. When that changes, the old pane gets `CSI O` and the new one `CSI I`, each only if its program has the mode on. The mode is read live.
		- Windows: the same bytes go to ConPTY. Since Windows 11 ConPTY turns the mode on itself and hands focus on to the console program. It wasn't checked on a Windows box.
	- Note: The minimap rule (G95) only reads the mode. Nothing there reads focus reports, so it's unchanged.
	- Verified:
		- Unit suite, clippy, and fmt pass.
		- In a window with 2 panes, each running a program that turns the mode on and logs what it reads: window out and back, a click into the other pane, then window out. Each program got `CSI I` and `CSI O` at the right moments, and a click on the pane that already had focus didn't send anything.
	- Swept: every place that moves pane focus (click, keyboard move, split, close, tab switch, menu, command line) is handled, since the holder is worked out in one place each pass rather than at those sites.
	- Branch: focusrep
	- Commit: 3d7e090
	- Test case: `a_program_that_asks_for_focus_changes_is_told` (ddxkd) and `focus_goes_out_of_one_pane_and_into_the_next` (ddxke), both seen failing before the fix.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: standard xterm behavior, tested.
	- Closed: 20261013-213659

- An old file with colors over a built-in theme shows the theme's colors after the update, when it has no machine test lines
	- ID: 2026101304551668
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Needs local test suite run?: No. Verified: 20261013, the unit suite, clippy, fmt, and the test ID check. The full pipeline hasn't run, so no dogfood build has it yet.
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261013-045516
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100910295901, 2026100907341818
	- Target OS: All
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- A config from before 10-09 with `theme: "Matrix"`, `colors.foreground` and `colors.cursor` set, and no `performance.rated_hardware` or remembered window lines.
		- Launch.
	- Incorrect behavior: the text shows Matrix's colors. The file's colors count as Custom's and show only when Custom is picked.
	- Expected behavior: the file's colors show over Matrix as its `*` changes, as they do for a file with those lines.
	- Reproduced: 20261013, a unit test with the file above. Adding a `rated_hardware` line makes the colors show.
	- Possible cause: `move_theme_colors` only runs from `move_state_out`, after its early return for a file without any state lines. The state lines are what mark a file from before 10-09, so moving it out needs another mark.
	- Actual cause: the move took an active state line as the only mark of an old file. A file written by hand doesn't have one, and neither does an old one whose state lines were deleted by hand.
	- Actual fix: There are 2 more marks, both read off the file. A file without a shcl Format line is old, since shcl 3.0 came before 10-09. The launch reads it before the step that adds the line. A state path on a commented line is old too, such as the old template's `# rated_hardware`, since the update drops those lines as well. An active state line still marks it, and only that one moves state out. A file this build wrote has the Format line and no state lines, so it's never moved again. The `kept` check still stops a second move after one that wrote.
	- Notes:
		- Nearly every real file has the machine test's lines, so this is mostly a hand-written file.
		- A file whose footer was deleted by hand reads as old, so its colors over a theme without any `*` changes would move again. A launch already reads such a file as shcl 2.x, makes its v2 backup and puts the footer back.
		- The last part of ddqwh is commented out. It used a file without a Format line as a file this build wrote. ddx9q checks a real one instead, written by a launch and saved.
	- Swept: the one place that decides a file is old for the move (`move_state_out`). Other old-file reads go line by line, such as the font switch in `fields::load`, and don't need a file mark. The launch path is the only caller (`load`, which `reload_from_disk` also runs).
	- Verified: ddx9q failed before the fix (the hand-written file didn't get any `*` changes) and passes after. With the Format line mark taken out it went red, with the commented line mark taken out it went red, and with the move always on it went red. Over 3 launches of a build with a hand-written file, the first wrote Matrix's `*` changes, and the second and third didn't change anything in the config.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261013: Question: is it OK that a hand-written file with no Format line counts as old? Answer (JC): yes.
	- Branch: oldcolors
	- Commit: a5e81f0
	- Test case: `an_old_file_with_no_state_lines_still_shows_its_colors_over_the_theme` (ddx9q). Test ddqwh was already there.
	- Acceptance signoff: JC, 20261013.
	- Closed: 20261013

- The scroll harness's altenter scene fails now and then when the box is busy
	- ID: 2026101307482605
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261013-074826
	- Opened by: CC
	- Target OS: Linux
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run the full pipeline while another build has the load average above 20.
	- Incorrect behavior: the X11 arm fails with "no output was easing when the alt screen took over, so nothing was tested", and the pipeline stops there.
	- Expected behavior: a timing miss is a skip, or the scene waits until the ease is running before it swaps the alt screen in.
	- Reproduced: 20261013, once in the full pipeline at load 15 to 23. A rerun of the harness alone right after, at the same load, passed every scene.
		- 20261013: before the fix, 6 of 6 runs of the scene alone failed this way with the harness and 16 busy processes pinned to the same 8 cores (load 19 to 22). With the same 16 spread over all 32 cores, 10 of 10 passed.
	- Notes:
		- The harness README calls this case a failure on purpose, since the scene tested nothing. Its short gap before the alt screen is fixed, so a slow frame can let the ease finish first.
	- Actual cause: the scene waited a fixed 0.25 s after its burst before it swapped the alt screen in. Even on a quiet box only 1 frame drew in that time. On a busy one none did, so the trace didn't show any ease before the swap.
	- Actual fix: the scene reads its own trace and swaps as soon as a frame shows the burst easing, waiting up to 10 s. When the wait runs out it leaves a note beside the trace, and the analyzer reports a skip instead of a fail. Without the note, no ease before the swap still fails. A skip beside passes exits 0, and fails under `--strict`.
	- Branch: altwait
	- Commit: 58176b7
	- Test case: scroll harness scene `altenter` (d9j4r), red 6 of 6 before the fix and green 10 of 10 after under the same load. There are 4 new note cases in `cicd/tests/scroll/verdict-test.bash` (dcbdt).
	- Verified: 20261013, under that load the scene passed 10 of 10 on X11 and 5 of 5 on Wayland, and the full X11 harness passed 12 of 12. With the load stopped, the full X11 harness passed 12 of 12 and the scene 6 of 6. With the alt-screen clamp taken out of `Scroll::set_max`, the scene failed 3 of 3 under load with the ease still running on the alt screen, so it still tests what it should after the repaint and clear changes. A 0 s wait gave the skip.
	- Sweep: the other scenes, for a fixed gap that a busy box can miss.
	- Swept: Only `altenter` swaps on a fixed gap that has to fall mid-ease. `clear` waits 3.8 s after its burst, and `chrome` and `aptbar` mark the frames to skip by the settle time in `run.bash`. Each passed under the same load, before and after.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: reproduced, the scene fails before the fix and passes after under the same load, and it still fails with the wobble put back.
	- Closed: 20261013-171405

	- Incorrect behavior: The box is 56 DIP wide whatever the font. "10080" fits at the default font with a few px to spare. A larger desktop font could cut it off, as it already could with 4 digits.
	- Expected behavior: The box is wide enough for the widest number its row allows, measured the way labels are.

	- Notes:
		- 20261008: Scaling the box with the font size was tried and dropped. It widened every box and shortened every slider at normal font sizes.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261008: Best guess. Every slider in the dialog gets one width, the widest any of them needs, so the sliders still end in one column. It's never narrower than the old 56 DIP, so nothing moves at an ordinary font unless a number needs more.
		- 20261008: Best guess. The width is the number plus the field's padding on both sides. The caret margin while typing is left out, since counting it would widen every box at the default font. A 5 digit number being typed still shows whole.
		- 20261008: Best guess. A wider box widens the panel's own floor, the way a long label does. The 9 tabs usually set the panel's width, so in practice the sliders give up the room.
	- Actual cause: The box width was a constant, and nothing measured the numbers.
	- Actual fix: The widest number each slider can show is measured in the dialog's own font: either end, the typed cap where a row has one, and for a decimal 99.94 and 999.9. The largest plus padding sets every number box, with 56 DIP as the floor. The UI style guide, the settings dialog design doc, and the spec file's note say so.
	- Swept: every fixed width box in the dialog. The color picker's value boxes and the dropdowns already grow with the font, and the hex, text, and path boxes stretch to the column.

In a real window at the default font, 1x is unchanged, apart from the caret blink and the Shell tab, which differ between 2 runs of the old build too. The panel stayed 707 wide at 1x and 1439 at 2x. At 2x the font comes out half a px larger per DIP, and "10080" needs 57 DIP, so every number box is 1 DIP wider and the sliders 1 DIP shorter. At 24 pt every number shows whole at 1x and 2x, the panel stays 1171 and 2342 wide, and the sliders are shorter by what the boxes gained.

	- Test case: `every_slider_number_fits_its_box_at_a_large_interface_font` (ddpa5), `a_wider_number_box_widens_the_panel_and_leaves_the_sliders` (ddpa6). Both fail with the box held at 56 DIP. The first also fails with the decimal bands taken out, the second with the panel ignoring the box.

- A test that measures Settings text before its first text context can measure in the wrong font
	- ID: 2026100909162017
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261009-091620
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100818102267, 2026100816465317, 2026100817355494
	- Target OS: All
	- Incorrect behavior: `every_slider_number_fits_its_box_at_a_large_interface_font` (ddpa5) and `a_focus_ring_takes_in_the_line_its_labels_are_on` (ddpc1) read the UI font's attributes before they make a text context. The family is chosen when the first context is made, so run alone, each measures its text in the fallback face while the layout uses the desktop's.
	- Expected behavior: each test measures in the face the layout was built from.
	- Reproduced: 20261009, by a probe run alone. The string "2026-10-09" measured 88.7 px that way, against 75.3 in the desktop's face. The 2 tests weren't run alone to see whether they pass for the wrong reason.
	- Possible cause: `ui_attrs()` reads the family a text context pins, and these tests call it once, ahead of the loop.
	- Reproduced: 20261013, each test run alone, here with GentiumAlt as the desktop font. Both passed. The slider test measured right only because the context's width memo, keyed by text alone, already had each number from the layout. The focus ring test measured the pair and radio labels ("Face", "Outline", "Scrim", "Stretch", "Zoom") in the fallback face at every size. The fallback is wider here, so it passed on a stricter number. A box with a narrower fallback could pass it wrongly. The probe string measured 222 px in the fallback against 191 in GentiumAlt.
	- Actual cause: The UI and terminal families, and their weights, are set only when a text context is built. Before the first one, `ui_attrs()`, `ui_bold_weight()`, `mono_attrs()` and `mono_bold_weight()` return the generic family and default weights. The app always builds a context before it draws or measures, so only tests hit it.
	- Actual fix: Whichever of those 4 is called first, before any context, sets the families itself, from a font system of its own, the same way a context does. After that they read what the last context set, as before. It's fixed in the one place, so both tests and any later one get the right face whatever order they read in.
	- Swept: every caller of the 4 functions. Tests that read them before a context: ddpa5 and ddpc1 (the 2 named), and dd5qf (`mono_attrs`, checks weights, measures nothing). Tests that read them after one: ddq87, ddq88, dd5ne, ddgh3, dd5qh. The text.rs tests that build their own font system set the family first. Every app caller is handed a text context, and `TextCtx::new_cpu` is the only place the app makes a font system. Nothing outside the code calls them.
	- Note: The fallback is still used where nothing resolves at all, as before. b26 doesn't name a desktop monospace font, so the terminal family comes from the built-in stack the same way for both paths. It wasn't run there.
	- Verified: 20261013, the new test fails with the fix taken out (the early attrs have the generic family) and passes with it. ddpa5, ddpc1, and the new test pass run alone. The merge gate (fmt, clippy, all 1272 unit tests), clippy for the Windows target, and the test ID check pass.
	- Branch: uifontmeasure
	- Commit: 140985b
	- Test case: `attrs_read_before_the_first_context_match_the_context` (ddwmh), which runs `attrs_before_context_child` (ddwmj) in a fresh copy of the test binary so no other test has set the families first.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: reproduced, the test fails before the fix and passes after, and only tests change behavior.
	- Closed: 20261013-050551

	- Reproduced: 20261008, before and after 2026100817355493.

- A failed test script's output is thrown away by the pipeline
	- ID: 2026100720280487
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261007-202804
	- Opened by: CC
	- Target OS: All
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Have any script test under `cicd/tests` fail during `cicd.bash`.
	- Incorrect behavior: `fRunTest` sends the script's output to `/dev/null`, so the log says only which test failed. A one-off failure can't be diagnosed after the fact. The test run folder test (ddazx) failed once that way on 20261007 and passed when run alone.
	- Expected behavior: a failed test's output ends up in the log or in a file the failure line names.
	- Actual cause: `fRunTest` and `fRunTest_MaySkip` both sent a test's stdout to `/dev/null`. Its stderr already went to the log.
	- Actual fix: A test's stdout goes to a file in the test run folder. A pass or a skip deletes it. A failure prints it to the log, the last 200 lines when it's longer, and the failure line names the file. The run folder is kept after a failed run, so the file is still there.
	- Swept: `cicd-win.ps1` runs its tests through `fExec`, which shows their output, so it doesn't have that pattern. Nothing else under `cicd` sends a test script's output to `/dev/null`, `$null`, or `Out-Null`. The private runner in `silkterm-private` drops only ssh output, never a test's. The NSIS step in both pipelines drops `makensis` output on a failure too, but it's a warning rather than a test, so it wasn't changed.
	- Verified: 20261008, `cicd/tests/testout/run.bash` failed 9 of 21 checks against the old `fRunTest` and passes now. `cicd/tests/engine/run.bash`, test IDs, shellcheck, and the bash style check pass.

- macOS: a Ctrl+click right after a window gets the focus acts as a plain click
	- ID: 2026100310321918
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Needs external testing:
		- b26: hold Ctrl and click into a SilkTerm window that doesn't have the focus. That first click opens the right-click menu. The same on a Settings dialog that doesn't have the focus.
		- b26: bring a window forward with Ctrl held, from the Dock or its title bar, then Ctrl+click in it before pressing anything else. The menu opens.
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261003-103219
	- Closed: 20261006-142958
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100220463754, 2026100220260471
	- Target OS: macOS
	- Test environment: b26
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Hold Ctrl, then click into a SilkTerm window or Settings that doesn't have the focus, or bring it forward with Ctrl still held and then click.
	- Incorrect behavior: The click is a plain left click. The window doesn't know Ctrl is down until a modifier key changes.
	- Expected behavior: A Ctrl+click opens the right-click menu, as it does once the window knows Ctrl is held.
	- Reproduced: No. It was read from winit 0.30.13's macOS code on 20261003. A window that gains the focus reports only that, without any held keys.
	- Possible cause: none found. winit 0.30.13 on macOS reads the held keys from each click, key press, and mouse move, from that event's own flags, and reports a change just before the event. The click that brings a window forward goes to the window, since SilkTerm leaves winit's first-click setting on. So a Ctrl+click on a window that just got the focus should already arrive with Ctrl held. It was read only, rather than seen on a Mac.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261003: No code changed. Seeding the held keys from the system when the focus arrives was weighed and left out. winit reports a change only against its own last value, which it clears when the window loses the focus. A Ctrl seeded that way and let go before any other event would never be reported, so it would stick, as in 2026100220463754.
		- 20261003: If b26 shows the bug anyway, the cause is elsewhere. `SILK_KEYDBG=1` prints each held-key and focus change for the terminal window, which is the next thing to look at.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261003: It should work as expected, where that is reasonably possible.
	- Actual fix: none, see the progress log.
	- Branch: mackeys
	- Test case: none. The gap would be in winit's macOS event code, which a test here can't drive. For the app's half, a left press with Ctrl held acts as a right press, and `ctrl_click_is_the_right_click_on_macos_only` tests it.

- macOS: the first frames after a window shows are drawn at the default size
	- ID: 2026100517535929
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Needs external testing: The `newwin` Windows scenario on vm925w, since every resize event now reads the window's size. A window resize and Settings on Wayland.
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261005-175359
	- Closed: 20261006-143038
	- Opened by: CC
	- Assigned to: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100514211602, 2026100114274893
	- Target OS: macOS
	- Test environment: b26
	- Incorrect behavior: For about 80 ms after a new window shows, its frames are drawn at 1000x640 points, while the window is already at its launch size.
	- Expected behavior: The first frame on screen is drawn at the window's size.
	- Reproduced: No. It was seen 20261005 on b26 in what the window reported about its size, rather than looked at on screen.
	- Possible cause: winit's `request_inner_size` returns nothing on macOS, though the window takes the size at once, so the surface waits for the resize event. A hidden window's frame is refused as occluded and the window is shown at once (2026100114274893), before that event comes.
	- Reproduced: Partly, 20261006 on b26. For about 85 ms after launch the surface was at the creation size, 2000x1280 pixels, while the window was already 2394x828, and the late resize from creation set it back to 2000x1280 once more. But no frame was drawn at that size in 6 launches. macOS refuses every frame until the window is on screen, about 110 ms in, and the real size has arrived by then. The Settings dialog was the same at its first size, 560x800.
	- Actual cause:
		- winit on macOS returns nothing when asked for a size, though the window takes it at once. So the surface stayed at the creation size until a resize event came.
		- The resize event from the window's creation comes after the real size is in place, and it moved the surface back to the creation size until the next one.
	- Actual fix:
		- A size request that winit returns nothing for still counts when the window already has a new size. The surface is made at the window's size before the first frame. Every size request goes through this, the dialogs' too.
		- A resize event sizes the surface at the window's own size rather than the event's, so a stale one doesn't change anything. The dialogs do the same.
		- 20261006: It's kept as a guard against the race, though no wrong frame was seen.
	- Swept: every `request_inner_size` call, 2 in app.rs and 6 in dialog.rs, and the 3 resize event handlers (window, dialog, notice).
	- Verified:
		- b26: 6 launches with the fix and 6 without, and Settings opened once each. With the fix the surface had the window's size from the start, and the late creation resize left it alone. Without it, the result was as under Reproduced.
		- Linux X11: `cicd/tests/startsize/run.bash` and `cicd/tests/wpresize/run.bash` pass, the unit tests pass, and Settings opened and resized under xfwm4 drew at its size.
	- Note: Windows and Wayland already report a requested size at once, and their resize events report the window's size, so nothing should change there. It wasn't run on either.
	- Branch: macfirst
	- Commit: 621d931
	- Test case: `a_size_the_window_took_without_saying_is_drawn_at` (ddk55), failing on the old code. The resize event half doesn't have a unit test, since it needs a real window.

	- ID: 2026100314050015

On b29w only consolemsg and _selftest ran. The rest skipped, since the console session there was locked.
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261003-140500
	- Closed: 20261006-143134
	- Opened by: CC
	- Target OS: Windows
	- Incorrect behavior:
		- All 164 functions are `fCamelCase`. None is Verb-Noun, so the approved-verb lint can never fire.
		- None of the scripts has comment-based help. Only 3 use `[CmdletBinding()]`. `install.ps1` has 2 untyped parameters.
		- There are 9 scripts that set `Set-StrictMode -Version 2.0` rather than Latest, with no reason given.
		- There are 29 calls that pass 3 or more positional arguments, and 5 use the `-EA` alias.
		- There are 8 loops that grow an array with `+=`.
	- Expected behavior: The scripts follow the PowerShell section of the directives.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261003: The naming half was open at first: rename to Verb-Noun, or record `fCamelCase` as a house allowance with its reason, the way Write-Host is.
		- 20261003: `PSUseApprovedVerbs` is now in the lint's excluded rules, with the reason beside it.
		- 20261006: Every script has comment-based help under its copyright lines, except the profile snippet. Small helper functions keep their one-line comments rather than a help block each.
		- 20261006: StrictMode is Latest where it was 2.0, and in the scripts that didn't have any: the job scripts, and the GUI harness, which sets it for its scenarios. A dot-sourced library leaves it to its caller. `shell_integration.ps1` runs in the user's own shell, so it doesn't have a help block and doesn't set anything.
		- 20261006: Every script with a param block has `[CmdletBinding()]`, and every script and function parameter is typed. Script block parameters were left alone.
		- 20261006: prerequisites.md and design.md say the dogfood launcher needs PowerShell 7, and it doesn't run on 5.1 today. Its changes keep to 5.1 syntax, but it wasn't made to run there.
		- 20261006: install.ps1 also got a fix. It failed at once when the shell running it had StrictMode on, which the `irm | iex` one-liner meets in a user's own session. It read a Path property that a script block doesn't have. Its `mv` is now called by path, which the lint on Windows flagged as Move-Item's alias.
		- 20261006: On Windows, 3 shell scan unit tests fail, apart from this item. They were filed as 2026100612422856.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261003: `fCamelCase` function names stay. They're an exception for this project only. The rest of the item stands.

- Code style: public items are commented with `//`, not `///`
	- ID: 2026100314050006
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261003-140500
	- Opened by: CC
	- Target OS: All
	- Incorrect behavior: Of about 900 public items outside the tests, 64 have a `///` doc. Another 531 have a plain `//` comment, and 304 don't have anything. `keys.rs`, `tabtitle.rs`, and `sysfont.rs` use `///`, but most other files don't. `shells.rs` and `fileassoc.rs` open with `//` where 23 other files use `//!`.
	- Expected behavior: The style guide says "Document public items with `///`".
	- Origin: c6eaa04 (2026-06-28) onward, in every file. There's no earlier review item. Confirmed.
	- Note: Most of the text already exists. The fix is mostly a change of comment form, then one line for the items without one. `buildnum.rs` stays on `//`, since `build.rs` includes it and `//!` wouldn't compile there.
	- Note: Code review 20261003 item 6.
	- Decisions:
		- The rule is about the form of a comment rather than whether one exists. A comment on anything declared `pub` is `///`, and a file's opening comment is `//!`. An item whose name says it all doesn't need a doc, since one would only repeat the name. The style guide says so now.
		- A note about a run of items, such as a group of colors, is a `///` on the first one. Its text reads the same in the source.
		- 20261006: Changed. A note over a run of items is a plain `//` right above them, with a blank line above the note, since a `///` belongs only to the item right below it. rustfmt takes out a blank line between a comment and a struct field, so the note can't have one under it. In all, 20 of them changed back, in config.rs, theme.rs, pane.rs, autotheme.rs, tip.rs, and xmp.rs. The docs check lets a `//` through when the next line is another pub item without a comment of its own.
		- Pub fields count too, since they are declared `pub` the same way. Enum variants and trailing `//` notes at a line's end are left as they are.
		- `missing_docs` can't do this, since on a bin crate it only asks for the crate's own doc.
	- Actual fix:
		- About 2,050 `//` lines on pub items and fields are now `///`, with the words unchanged. Items with a doc went from 67 to 641 of 938. Fields with one went from 5 to 79.
		- The opening comments of 16 files are `//!`, including build.rs and the 2 test crates. `buildnum.rs` keeps `//`.
		- Of the items without a comment, 11 got one short line, where the name hid something: the 3 `take_*` calls in config.rs, `click_select`, `note_history`, `WakeGate::handled`, and 5 more. There are 297 items that stay without one.
		- The 2 lint reasons that sat above their attribute moved into `reason = "..."`, on `TermInstance::spawn` and `shells::Group`.
		- The 2 notes in palette.rs that a blank line had cut off from their function are joined back on.
		- New docs set off `doc_markdown` in about 140 places, which were fixed with backticks. `SilkTerm` and a few key names are listed in clippy.toml as words. In 2 lines that began with a dash, the dash read as a list, so it moved to the line above. `cargo doc` warned on `<shell>` style text in 2 places, which are now in backticks.
	- Test case: `cicd/tests/docs/run.py` (dd5nv) now fails on a plain `//` line above a pub item or field, past its attributes, outside test code, and on an opening comment that isn't `//!`. It failed on 2,053 lines and 16 files on the old tree and passes after. Planting one `//` line above `shells::Group`'s attributes turned it red again.
	- Verified: clippy clean for Linux, `--features profiling`, Windows, and macOS targets, `cargo doc` with private items, rustfmt, the full unit suite (1147 passed), test ID check, and Python lint.

- Code style: the benchmark scripts catch every exception
	- ID: 2026100512570726
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261005-125707
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100314050016
	- Target OS: All
	- Incorrect behavior: `termbench.py` has 7 `except Exception:` blocks and `sizebench-classify.py` has 4, so a typo or a bad read is swallowed the same as the error each one expects.
	- Expected behavior: Each catches the exceptions it means to, per the Python section of the style directives.
	- Note: It was found while working 2026100314050016, which didn't include it.
	- Origin: The scripts as first written, termbench.py and sizebench-classify.py on 20260728 and 20260730. Confirmed, since the new rule finds all 11.
	- Actual fix:
		- `ruff.toml` turns on BLE001, so an `except Exception` fails the lint stage. A catch-all meant as one takes `# noqa: BLE001` with a reason. None of the 11 needed it.
		- Each catch names the errors its code can raise: `OSError`, `ValueError` for bad numbers and undecodable output, `IndexError`, `subprocess.SubprocessError` for a timeout, `OverflowError` for a bad timestamp, and `ctypes.ArgumentError` for a Windows call.
		- termbench's raw mode turns `termios.error`, which isn't an `OSError`, into one, since the caller can't name it on Windows. Putting the tty back still ignores a tty that's gone.
		- termbench still parses as Python 3.8. The style guide's Python section names the rule.
	- Swept: `grep -rn "except Exception\|except:\|except BaseException"` over every tracked `.py` outside `forks/` finds nothing else, and the lint over the whole tree passes.
	- Test case: `cicd/tests/pylint/run.bash` (ddgkn) has a case for BLE001, and one for a catch-all marked with noqa. The lint over the tree in stage 3 is the other half.
	- Verified:
		- The lint fails the old scripts with exactly the 11 findings, and passes now. The pylint test fails the new case against the old `ruff.toml` and passes against the new one.
		- Same output, old against new, on Linux: every narrowed path driven into its expected errors (missing pid or program, timeout, undecodable output, bad timestamp, no objdump, no tty, a tty closed before exit), a real size reading of a process with 10 libraries, and the self-check within its usual drift. On b29w the Windows console, grid, memory counter, and version probes match too.
		- A full termbench run with stdin closed refuses before raw mode, the same message and exit code both ways.
		- The showdown, rigs, and docs tests pass.

- A Settings save on a config that was deleted while running says it saved and writes nothing
	- ID: 2026100316135866
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261003-161358
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100315581313
	- Target OS: All
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Launch, then delete the config file.
		- Change a setting in Settings and press OK, or resize the window.
	- Incorrect behavior: The dialog closes as if it saved. Nothing is written, and the next launch starts from the defaults.
	- Expected behavior: The save writes the file, or says it didn't.
	- Reproduced: No. It was found by reading `persist` while working 2026100315581313.
		- 20261004 on b23: a unit test deleted the file and saved through `persist`, once with a Settings edit and once with a window size change. Both reported that they saved, but didn't write anything.
	- Actual cause: `persist` took a missing file as nothing to do and reported that it saved.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261004: The save writes a full new config file from the template with the current settings, the same as a first launch would, and goes through quietly without a notice.
	- Actual fix:
		- A save that finds the file gone makes its folder and starts from the template. It keeps every setting the file had when the program last read or wrote it, then puts the save's own change on top. The copy is done the same way as for a fresh file from `upgrade`.
		- Values that last only the session stay out of the new file, such as a rotated wallpaper or a font given on the command line. The save still writes only what changed against what the window loaded.
		- The shell list is still three-way against the file. The new file has the list, so no entry reads as removed. A file the program never saw gets the list the window loaded.
		- Like any fresh file from the template, the new one doesn't keep the old file's comments or layout, or a line the template doesn't have a place for.
		- Only the settings file counts as the file last seen. A shell profile goes through the same writer, and the one written at launch used to take its place, so the save started from the bare template.
	- Swept: Every caller of `persist`: Settings OK, window size, font zoom and per-monitor sizes, the copy, minimap and single tab toggles, and shells found at launch. The revert arrow's write and the cleared font's write run after `persist`, so they find the new file. The rating write still says it couldn't read a missing file, so it doesn't claim to have saved. That was left alone. The launch steps run after a launch lays the template down.
	- Test case: `a_save_on_a_deleted_file_writes_it_new` (ddg6v) and `a_save_on_a_deleted_file_keeps_the_shell_list` (ddg6w). Both fail with the old answer put back and pass now. The first also fails when the save starts from the bare template without the old settings. `cicd/tests/delcfg/run.bash` (ddhms), in the pipeline, and `a_save_on_a_deleted_file_keeps_it_after_a_profile_write` (ddhmt). Both fail on the old code.
	- Verified: The unit suite passes, 1085 tests. fmt is clean, clippy is clean for Linux and Windows, and the test ID check passes. It wasn't checked in a real window. The 2 app-side callers were read rather than run.
	- Verified: 20261005 on b23, in a real window: after the delete, a resize and Ctrl+Plus each wrote a new file with the old file's settings and the new value. Before the profile fix it didn't keep any of them.
	- Branch: delcfg, signoff
	- Commit: 312f355, 9319ff2
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: reproduced in a real window, fixed, and pinned by a pipeline test.
	- Closed: 20261005-094503

	- ID: 2026100314050010
	- Type: Bug

	- Opened by: CC
	- Target OS: All
	- Incorrect behavior:
		- About 40 `unwrap` or `expect` calls outside the tests don't give a reason. They're the settings store at config.rs 831 and 1171, 5 lock unwraps in perf.rs, 4 in text.rs, `NonZeroU32::new(..).unwrap()` in gfx.rs, 8 env reads in build.rs, and 2 on the chrome cache in app.rs.
		- text.rs repeats one `expect` message 7 times.
		- A poisoned lock is unwrapped in some places, skipped with `.ok()` in others, and taken with `PoisonError::into_inner` in a third set, sometimes in one file.
		- In cwd.rs and profile.rs, 7 `unsafe` blocks don't have a `// SAFETY:` line, where about 25 others do.
		- main.rs reads `SILK_PROFILE_OUT` a second time and unwraps it, after reading and dropping it 10 lines up.

Every std lock goes through it. The term lock is a `FairMutex` that doesn't poison, so its try-then-lock order is untouched (G2).
		- clippy's `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, and `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` are on. Tests are exempt through `clippy.toml`. Each unwrap left outside the tests has an allow with its reason, 10 in all, and the GL diagnostic probe allows both for the whole file.
		- The rest were removed: the gfx.rs `NonZeroU32` unwraps, 2 of the 4 chrome cache unwraps in app.rs, build.rs's file reads and writes (now `?`, with one `cargo_env` for the variables cargo always sets), and the profiler's expects in main.rs, which now keep the path from the first `SILK_PROFILE_OUT` read. text.rs has one message and 2 helpers in place of 7 copies.
		- Every unsafe block has a `// SAFETY:` line, the 7 in cwd.rs and profile.rs and the 28 more the lint found in ctl.rs, gfx.rs, term.rs, dialog.rs, and sysfont.rs. A few existing comments only moved to where the lint reads them.
		- A failure in the profiler build or in build.rs now ends with an error message where it panicked before. Nothing else changes.
	- Swept:
		- Every `.lock()`, `.read()`, and `.write()` on a std lock outside the tests, in config.rs, cwd.rs, perf.rs, shells.rs, term.rs, and text.rs, plus the test-only `PoisonError::into_inner` calls in config.rs. Test code still unwraps its own locks.
		- Unwraps and unsafe blocks: clippy with the 3 lints on Linux, Windows, macOS, and the profiling feature, all targets.

- The pipeline starts a process per item in 2 loops
	- ID: 2026100314050014
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Needs local test suite run?: No
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261003-140500
	- Opened by: CC
	- Target OS: Linux
	- Incorrect behavior:
		- cicd.bash `fInUse` runs `readlink` once for every process on the box, about 1,500 here. It runs once per dogfood destination that already has a file, so up to about 4,500 forks per full run.
		- gfs-rotate.bash starts about 10 `date` and `basename` processes per file it rotates, twice per run.
	- Expected behavior: There's no fork per item in a loop. `[[ "${exe}" -ef "${want}" ]]` does the first check as a builtin. `printf '%(...)T'` and `${f##*/}` do the second.
	- Note: gfs-rotate.bash is a shared helper, so the fix goes to its canonical copy too, which is outside this tree.
	- Origin: 9ac3d4b (2026-09-26) for `fInUse`, b887d3d (2026-06-28) for gfs-rotate. There's no earlier review item. Confirmed for the fork count, but the time isn't measured.
	- Reproduced: 20261004. Over a stand-in list of 2000 processes the old `fInUse` started 3,432 processes, 2 for each one with an exe. Rotating 200 files started 2,446 beyond the rm and mv it reports.
	- Actual fix:
		- `fInUse` tests each process with `-ef`, a builtin. Only a process running that same file goes on to the old readlink compare, so a hard link under another name still doesn't count. A file deleted and replaced while its old copy runs still isn't in use.
		- gfs-rotate works out a name's date with arithmetic and writes stamps and period keys with `printf '%(...)T'`. A time a clock change repeats gets the same instant date gave, and one it skips still falls back to the mtime. `basename` became `${f##*/}`.
		- The canonical gfs-rotate.bash got the same hunks. Before the change it differed from this copy only in one comment word, "labelled", which it keeps.
	- Swept: `fInUse` is the only /proc scan in the pipeline. `fOwnedRoot` in `utility/include/bench-common.bash` reads only the few processes a benchmark started, so it was left alone. `fNewest` in `cicd/utility/lint-report.bash` ran `basename` per run log and now uses `${f##*/}`, with the same output. The shcl clones under `forks/` have their own gfs-rotate copies and belong to that project.
	- Note: These were left alone. A name without a date still costs one fork for its mtime, but only once, since a kept file is renamed to one with a date. The rm or mv per changed file stays, since batching them could change which of 2 same-stamp files gets a name.
	- Verified: 20261004. Both tests below pass, and both fail with the old code put back. Old and new gfs-rotate gave the same output and left the same files for 300 dated files, 3 runs each, in 4 time zones, and gave the same date for 429 names in 11 zones. Shellcheck is clean at the gate's level, and the test ID check passes.
	- Branch: nofork
	- Commit: 54436fb
	- Test case: `cicd/tests/engine/run.bash` (dd5nn), "and 2000 processes cost a few forks, not one each", plus the new hard link and replaced file checks. `cicd/tests/rotate/run.bash` (dd5nq), "names are read and stamps written the way date does it" and "rotating 200 files costs a few forks beyond the files it changes". Both count forks exactly through `cicd/tests/_forks.bash`, or box-wide with a looser limit where that can't be done.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: reproduced, tests fail before and pass after, and the output is unchanged.
	- Closed: 20261004-151110
	- Note: Code review 20261003 item 14.

- The launch names an unreadable line 2 lines short of where the file has it
	- ID: 2026100115322366
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261001-153223
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100115322364
	- Target OS: All
	- Test environment: b23
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Start with `--config` on a 3-line file: `window:`, `\t\topacity: 1.0`, `\tmargin: 4`.
	- Incorrect behavior: the console says line 198, and the margin line is at 200 in the file after the launch.
	- Expected behavior: the console names the line number the file has.
	- Reproduced: 20261001 on b23, with this branch and with the beta3 build. The Windows notice gives the right number.
	- Actual cause:
		- shcl isn't the cause. The launch prints its messages once its own rewrites are done, and the line numbers are right for the file at that moment.
		- The performance rating then writes `profile:` and `rated_hardware:` into the `performance:` block at the top, once the window is up. That moves every line below it down by 2.
		- The Windows notice is worked out at the moment a save is refused, so it sees the file as it is then.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261001: It was reproduced on the real program. The console said 198, and the file had the line at 200. The rating wrote the 2 extra lines.
		- 20261002: A second, corrected message is used rather than holding the messages until the rating has written. See Decisions. The next shcl beta might help.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261002: The second message stays for now. The clean fix is for the rating to fill in the template's commented `profile:` and `rated_hardware:` lines where they are, so no line moves and the first message is right. shcl's keep-lines save can't do that yet, so it's filed as 2026100219054510. Holding the messages for the rating was turned down, since they could come late, or never if the window closes first.
	- Actual fix:
		- The launch keeps what it printed about the file. A later write to the same file prints again whatever now reads differently, so the last message names the line the file has. The first one still names the old number.
		- On the real program the console now ends with line 200, where the file has it.
	- Swept: all 3 kinds of launch message go through the restate. They're the unreadable-line and spelling notes, shcl's own errors, and the bad-value and set-twice notes. Every write goes through the one writer, so the rating, the shell list, and a Settings save all get it.
	- Branch: cfglines

	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: hard to check by hand, and its test failed before the fix and passes on dev.
	- Closed: 20261003-124705

- Alt+Super plus a letter opens an in-window menu, as Alt plus a letter does
	- ID: 2026100311020484
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261003-110204
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100220292607
	- Target OS: Linux, Windows
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- With the menu bar shown, hold Alt and Super and press the letter of a menu title, such as F.
	- Incorrect behavior: The menu opens, as if only Alt were held.
	- Expected behavior: A chord with Super held isn't a menu shortcut.
	- Reproduced: No. It was seen in a unit test on 20261003, `the_command_chords_are_the_only_program_chords_on_macos`, which now allows it off a Mac.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261003: Alt+Shift plus a letter doesn't open a menu either. Only Alt alone does.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261003: It was closed with Alt alone or Alt+Shift opening a menu, and then reopened because of the decision above.
	- Actual cause: The menu letter check asked only that Alt was held and Ctrl wasn't, so Super held as well still counted.
	- Actual fix:
		- One check, `opens_menu_title` in input.rs, says a letter is a menu title only with Alt alone. The title underlines shown while Alt is held use it too, so they show only with Alt alone.
		- The UI/UX style guide says so under the menu chords.
		- `the_command_chords_are_the_only_program_chords_on_macos` is back to its strict form. A Command chord doesn't do anything off a Mac.
	- Swept:
		- 20261003: The menu title letter and the title underlines both go through `opens_menu_title`, now Alt alone. The Alt+Shift pane chords in keys.rs are bound chords, which come before the menu title, so they're unchanged. The Settings dialog's Alt button letters use their own check, which was left as is. No doc, glossary, or design doc said Alt+Shift opens a menu. The code comments that said so were fixed.
		- The menu title letter (`hotkey_in`, which `hotkey_on` and `hotkey_for` both call) and the title underlines in app.rs were both fixed. The bound chords in keys.rs, including the Alt+Shift pane chords, already match the exact set of Ctrl, Alt, Shift, and Command held. A bare Alt press doesn't open the menu bar, and Alt alone only shows the underlines. A letter typed with a menu already open picks its row whatever is held, which was left as is.
	- Verified: 20261003, the unit tests, fmt, and clippy for Linux, Windows, and macOS.
	- Branch: altsuper, then altonly

- A cursor blink or fade can wait for an unrelated event, like the minimap's redraw did
	- ID: 2026092821452948
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20260928-214529
	- Opened by: CC
	- Assigned to: CC
	- Target OS: All
	- Incorrect behavior: `about_to_wait` collects each pane's cursor wake before the frame is drawn. A wake the frame itself sets isn't seen until something else wakes the loop.
	- Expected behavior: A wake set while drawing is honored on time.
	- Reproduced: No. It was read from the code while fixing the minimap's version of the same gap, which waited up to 2 seconds when idle.
	- Related IDs: the done old-format item "Minimap: with a very deep scrollback, redrawing the map under heavy output stops the terminal for a moment each time".
	- Actual cause:
		- A cursor that parks sets its resume time in the frame. The loop read that time before drawing, so a cursor that parked in the frame didn't have a wake at all, and one whose resume moved earlier kept the old time.
		- The same order affected 4 window wakes. The idle release and the rating banner were missed when the frame revealed the window or a rating ended. The rating's start waited for its cap when the wallpaper showed in the frame. A frame asked for after drawing, when a rating ended or stepped the profile down, waited for the next event.
	- Progress log:
		- 20260929: It wasn't seen on screen. It was checked by unit test and clippy on b23 only.
	- Actual fix: Every pane wake, the cursor's and the minimap's, is read after the frame from one list (`PaneWakes`). The idle release, the rating's start and banner, and the reveal deadline are read after it too. A frame asked for after drawing is drawn on the next pass.
	- Branch: curwake
	- Test case: `a_wake_set_while_drawing_is_kept` (dd9nh). It was seen to fail with only the minimap's wake read after the frame. The window wakes don't have a test, since they're in the event loop.
	- Swept: every wake `about_to_wait` waits on. Per pane, the cursor and the minimap. Per window, the capture, dialog, dialog raise, idle release, restored title, second heal, wallpaper rotation, shell scan, tab tip, rating start and banner, reveal, and VRAM probe wakes. The ones not listed in the fix were already read after the frame, or the frame doesn't set them.
	- Closed: 20260930-153118

	- Reproduced: 20261013 on b23, in the full pipeline run at 3e8df3f.
	- Actual cause: the size comes from `du -h`, which on ZFS reads a just-written file as almost nothing until the write is committed, and after that gives the compressed size, 7.0M here.

	- Test case: none, since it only changes a printed size. The next pipeline run shows it.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: mechanical

- Windows: a tab keeps naming a program started from cmd after it exits
	- ID: 2026101407014142
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Done
	- Severity: Low
	- Opened: 20261014-070141
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026100907341819
	- Target OS: Windows
	- Test environment: b29w
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Open a window with cmd as its shell.
		- Run `silkterm --wallpaper <file> & cls`.
	- Incorrect behavior: The tab reads `Windows Cmd [silkterm]` after the command is done and cmd is back at its prompt.
	- Expected behavior: The tab doesn't name a program once cmd is back at its prompt.
	- Reproduced: 20261014 on b29w, in the `livecfg` scenario's shot of window E.
		- 20261014 on b29w: Confirmed with a small program that sleeps 3 seconds and doesn't have a console. Run from cmd, the tab read `[nap]` while it ran and still did 2 seconds after it ended. Clicking the window and pressing a key changed it to `[last: nap]`.
	- Possible cause: cmd doesn't wait for a GUI program, so `cls` ran while silkterm.exe was still alive. On Windows the program is a live child of the shell, kept until the terminal stirs (G38). Nothing stirs after the `cls`, so the old answer stays. It wasn't confirmed.
	- Actual cause: As above. The cached answer waits for output or a key, and a program cmd didn't wait for ends after the prompt, without anything printed.
	- Actual fix: The child the probe names is watched by the system's thread pool. When it ends the pane is told, and the next frame asks again.
		- Cost: there's no polling. Each command found takes one process handle and one wait, and its end takes one event plus one more look at the process list. That look would have come at the next key anyway.
	- Note: Once it ends the tab reads `[last: <program>]`, as after any other command.
	- Verified:
		- The new Windows scenario `cmdgui` failed on dev and passes on the branch, where the tab read `[last: nap]` without anything typed. `livecfg`'s window E now reads `Windows Cmd [last: silkterm]`.
		- `a_watched_command_says_when_it_ends` passes on b29w and fails with the wait's callback emptied. Unit suite, clippy for Linux and Windows, and fmt pass.
	- Swept: `command_child` is the one probe on Windows. It feeds the tab label, the minimap's running program, and copy-output's at-prompt check, so all 3 get the news. From reading the code, copy-output also stayed armed for such a command until the next key. Unix asks the foreground process group, which a program the shell didn't wait for isn't in.
	- Branch: conpty
	- Commit: ca25198
	- Test case: `a_watched_command_says_when_it_ends` (ddy7y), seen failing with the callback emptied; wingui scenario `cmdgui` (ddy7c), seen failing on dev.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: cause confirmed, red before and green after on b29w.
	- Closed: 20261014-083844
