- A drag select recomposes the minimap about 11 times a second, though the map shows no selection
	- ID: 2026102407065861
	- Type: Enhancement
	- Status: Done
	- Needs hand testing: With the map on, a drag select, a link hover, typing on the prompt line, and a color change in Settings, all in a real window.
	- Stand-in: none (20261028). The machine part already ran: ddkre and the scroll harness passed at e95b81b. What's left is how the map looks.
		- 20261025: The dogfood pool now has build dedvg, from dev at a9daddc, for Linux and Windows, with the fixes from 10-24 and 10-25. A window started before the next launch still runs de5r9.
	- Priority: Low
	- Opened: 20261024-070658
	- Opened by: CC
	- Related IDs: 2026102321230038, 2026102407065855
	- Target OS: All
	- Requirements:
		- A pane rebuild that changes nothing the map shows, such as a selection change, doesn't recompose the map.
		- Typing on the prompt line, output, a scroll, a resize, and a color change still update the map.
	- Notes:
		- `Pane::build` calls `map.update` on every forced rebuild, and that composes whenever the 90 ms gap is up. A drag rebuilds every frame, so the map composes on every frame past the gap. That costs about 20 allocations a time on b23, plus the compose's own CPU.
		- The due compose is also what picks up a changed screen row without new history, so skipping it needs some other sign the screen's text changed. `last_rows` already has a hash per row.
		- ddkre's drag limit has the compose in every frame, so this lowers its figure.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261024: It's done by where the rebuild comes from, rather than by a hash of the screen. A moved selection and a link hover probe now mark the window with their own flag. The panes draw again as before, but the map is only updated for the window's other causes, a pane's own output and its scroll. So typing, output, a scroll, a resize, and a color change take the same path to the map as before.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261024: The selection alone wasn't enough. A pointer moving over text also starts a link hover probe, which marked the whole window, so both panes still composed on every drag frame. The hover probe takes the same flag now.
		- 20261025: Verified: the scroll harness on X11 and on Wayland (d9j4r) and the allocations per frame test (ddkre) passed in the full run at e95b81b, and in the gate. Only the hand look is left.
		- 20261026: ddkre and the scroll harness on X11 and Wayland (d9j4r) passed again at fab6815.
		- 20261028: ddkre and the scroll harness on X11 and Wayland (d9j4r) passed again at 64f3584.
		- 20261105: ddkre now counts map composes too, and fails on any at rest or in the drag (closetests, 0a83ff6). It read 0 and 0. - Wayland: a copy a program sends while no SilkTerm window has focus is dropped
	- ID: 2026101607585700
	- Type: Enhancement
	- Status: Done
	- Priority: Low
	- Opened: 20261016-075857
	- Opened by: JC
	- Related IDs: 2026101509024607
	- Target OS: Linux
	- Test environment: Headless sway on b23, without DISPLAY and with DISPLAY set.
	- Requirements:
		- Hold the copy, and set the clipboard when that SilkTerm window gets the focus again.
		- A line in usage.md saying a copy made from a window without focus on Wayland waits for it to get focus.
	- Notes:
		- Wayland lets a window set the clipboard only while it has the keyboard. X11 doesn't have that limit, and stays as it is.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261103: It's the clipboard crate's own worker that drops the store, when its seat doesn't have a keyboard. The compositor never sees it.
		- 20261103: A window on a workspace out of view doesn't read any output, so its store only arrives once it's shown and has the keyboard again. The case that lost a copy was a window on screen with another one in front.
		- 20261103: The window also doesn't have the keyboard for a moment after it opens, while it already counted as focused. A store then was dropped too, and is held now.
	- Decisions:
		- 20261103: The clipboard keeps its own idea of whether the window has the keyboard, starting without it on Wayland, rather than reading the window's focus flag, which starts out true.
		- 20261103: Only the last store per selection is held. A copy a person makes meanwhile, such as in Settings, replaces the held one, so a held store never overwrites a newer copy made in SilkTerm.
		- 20261103: While a dialog has the keyboard, a program's store waits for the terminal window too. A dialog is modal, so the terminal gets focus back when it closes.
		- 20261103: The test takes a second window from `foot`, which sway tiles beside SilkTerm, so the window stays on screen. foot is now one of the tools the test needs.
	- Swept: Every place a program sets a selection: OSC 52 to the clipboard and to the primary, both through the one handler. Copy on select, copy on output, the chords, and the dialogs all run with the keyboard, and set at once as before. X11, macOS, and Windows set at once too.
	- Branch: rnd1104
	- Commit: 6b138b0
	- Test case: `cicd/tests/wlclip/run.bash` (ddzwc), with a second window taking the keyboard: both stores wait, then go through on focus. The 4 new checks failed with the hold switched off and pass with it, also with the cores loaded. Unit tests dev22, dev23, dev24, and dev25 check that a store is held until focus, also before the first focus, that the last one wins, that a newer copy wins, and that X11 is unchanged.
	- Verified:
		- 20261103: wlclip passes 23 of 23 on the final code, also without a wait after launch. An earlier form of the same hold passed 3 times, once at load 36 on 32 cores.
		- 20261103: Gate: fmt, clippy, scripts, and docs pass, and clippy for Windows and macOS is clean. Tests: 1428 pass, and the 1 failure is ddghe on `cicd/tests/herdback/_wmmove.py`, from another item's commit.
	- Acceptance signoff: Self-closed: the store is held and set on focus, the test fails before and passes after, and X11 is unchanged.
	- Closed: 20261103-193225

- Windows Terminal handoff
	- ID: 2026092810510800
	- Type: Feature
	- Status: Canceled
	- Priority|Severity: Avg
	- Opened: 20260928-105138
	- Opened by: JC
	- Assigned to: JC
	- Target OS: Windows
	- Test environment:
	- Version and build:
	- Requirements:
		- In order to register as the "default terminal" in Windows, several unusual things are required.
		- I closed the webpage that describes exactly what, before copying the URL, so do research again.
		- Open questions:
			- Generally, I'd like the ability for the user to be able to register the one installed version of SilkTerm as the default terminal.
			- But for me specifically, I'd like to be able to register 'n8runterm' as the default. (Is that a completely separate thing?)
	- Estimated effort: Avg
	- Actual effort:
	- Progress log:
		- 20260928: Research so far, moved here from a second copy of this item:
			- Windows: let SilkTerm be picked as the default terminal, so a console program started from anywhere, such as double-clicking a `.bat`, opens in SilkTerm instead of conhost or Windows Terminal.
			- There isn't a setting or script that can do this from the outside. Windows stores the choice in `HKCU\Console\%%Startup` as 2 COM class IDs, `DelegationConsole` and `DelegationTerminal`, rather than as program paths. The console host creates that class and calls `ITerminalHandoff::EstablishPtyHandoff`, passing over the pipes of a program that's already running.
				- 20260930: It takes 2 hops. The built-in conhost only knows `IConsoleHandoff`, and passes the session to the `DelegationConsole` class. That one, Windows Terminal's OpenConsole, then calls `ITerminalHandoff3` on the `DelegationTerminal` class. It was checked in the microsoft/terminal source, and in the conhost and OpenConsole binaries on vm925w.
			- Checked 2026-09-28: the source doesn't have anything for this, and neither does build `slktrmdf_20260927-175446_gnulwi`. Pointing the registry at SilkTerm today would break every console launch.
				- 20260930: A failed handoff falls back to conhost, so it isn't a hard break. But COM waits up to 60 seconds for the class to appear, and each launch would also open a plain SilkTerm window, so in practice it's close to the same. It was read from the source rather than tried.
			- Add a COM local server to SilkTerm that implements the handoff interface. It's defined in microsoft/terminal at `src/host/proxy/ITerminalHandoff.idl`. Newer builds call `ITerminalHandoff3`, so check which version the current console host uses before starting.
				- 20260930: Confirmed. OpenConsole calls only `ITerminalHandoff3` since Windows Terminal 1.22, and conhost never calls any of them. The OpenConsole in Windows Terminal 1.24 on vm925w has only that interface's ID.
			- Give the pty backend a second way in. Today it always creates its own ConPTY. A handed-off session arrives with its pipes, signal pipe, and process handles already made, and the tab has to run those.
				- 20260930: With version 3, the terminal makes the 2 data pipes and gives the console host its ends. The signal pipe, a session reference, and the console host and client process handles arrive ready-made. Resize is a 6-byte packet on the signal pipe, and closing the session is closing those handles, so it doesn't need `conpty.dll`.
			- Register the class under `HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{guid}\LocalServer32`, pointing at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\silkterm.exe` with a flag like `--handoff`. That's the symlink the launcher keeps pointed at the newest dogfood build, so the default follows each new build.
				- A handed-off window skips the launcher, so it won't be elevated.
					- 20260930: An elevated console program doesn't hand off at all, and stays in conhost. Windows Terminal has the same limit, by design (microsoft/terminal#10276).
				- 20260930: COM adds ` -Embedding` to the command line on its own, so no flag of ours is needed. The program it starts has 60 seconds to register the class.
			- Find out what `DelegationConsole` has to be. The belief is that Windows Terminal's OpenConsole, `{2EACA947-7F5F-4CFA-BA87-8F7FBEEFBE69}`, is what passes a session on to a third-party terminal that the built-in conhost doesn't. It wasn't verified. The ConPTY redistributable already being tried here includes its own console host, which may or may not be usable for this.
				- 20260930: Verified. It has to be Windows Terminal's OpenConsole, with that ID. Conhost's own ID turns handoff off, and conhost can't reach a terminal by itself. So Windows Terminal has to be installed. It also has the parts that pass the call between processes. The redistributable's OpenConsole has the same ID built in, so it can't stand in as a second console host.
			- Add a way to switch it on and off, either in Settings or as a command-line option. Turning it off means setting both values back to all zeros, which is "Let Windows decide".
				- 20260930: A missing value means the same. The account on vm925w has Windows Terminal set by name, though, so off may be better as putting back whatever was there. See the open points below.
			- The Settings app's dropdown only lists packaged apps that declare the handoff extension. An unpackaged SilkTerm could still write the registry values itself, but it would never show up in that list.
				- 20260930: It takes 2 app extensions in the same package, `com.microsoft.windows.console.host` and `com.microsoft.windows.terminal.host`, so a packaged SilkTerm has to name a console host too. For a pair it doesn't know, Windows Terminal's own Settings page shows "Let Windows decide".
		- 20260930: The research was redone against the microsoft/terminal source and docs, and checked read-only on vm925w (Windows 11 25H2, Windows Terminal 1.24). Corrections are the dated sub-bullets above. The plan is in details.md, under "Windows Terminal handoff plan (20260930)".
		- 20260930: No other terminal has released this yet. WezTerm has 2 open requests (wezterm#7534, wezterm#7328). A few small projects have code, 2 of them in Rust, and all take the same route: Windows Terminal's OpenConsole as the console host, and their own class as the terminal.
		- 20260930: `n8runterm` isn't a separate thing. The registration names a program, and COM starts it by itself. The launcher could be named there, but then PowerShell, and by default a UAC prompt, would come before every console launch. The launcher already keeps `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\silkterm.exe` pointed at the newest build, so registering that path gets the same result without it.
		- 20260930: Left undecided, and moot since the item is canceled:
			- Whether to rely on Windows Terminal being installed. It's what passes the session on. Doing without it means building our own console host and bundling it, which is much bigger.
			- Whether a handed-off program opens in a new SilkTerm window each time, like conhost, or as a tab in a window that's already open, like Windows Terminal. The plan starts with a new window.
			- Whether the handed-off program's tab closes right away when it exits, as panes and conhost both do now, or stays open with the exit status, as `--keep-open` does.
			- Whether the switch is a command-line option only at first, or a Settings row too.
			- Whether switching it off puts back whatever was set before, or always "Let Windows decide".
			- Whether to register it for the test account on vm925w while testing. It would write that account's console and class keys, and put them back after each run.
	- Decisions:
		- 20260930: Canceled for good, and not to be revisited. That includes the COM handoff and any console host of our own. Being the default terminal takes a server that adopts a live console session, and it needs Windows Terminal installed. File associations handle the cases that matter for a small part of the work.
	- Branch: wthandoff
	- Commit:
	- Test case: None, since it was canceled.
	- Acceptance signoff:
	- Superseded by ID: 2026093009280571
	- Closed: 20260930-092805

SwiftShader's Vulkan driver, as Chrome bundles it, gave a CPU device once wgpu's `vulkan-portability` feature was on. SilkTerm came up on it and started its shells, but every frame was dropped, since the Metal layer it draws to doesn't have a device to give a picture with.
		- 20261103: So a fix needs the libraries in the Mac app and a second way to show a frame, drawn off screen and copied back. That's too big for one pass. It gets split once the question is answered.

	- Branch: rnd1103

- top quits smooth scrolling at some point
	- ID: 2026101310563310
	- Type: Bug
	- Status: Moot
	- Severity: Avg
	- Opened: 20261013-105632
	- Opened by: JC
	- Target OS: All
	- Version and build: Seen in the 10-10 dogfood build (ddrka), with top running since the evening before.
	- Steps to reproduce:
		- Run `top` and leave it running.
	- Incorrect behavior: top quits smooth scrolling at some point.
	- Expected behavior: Smooth scrolling keeps working however long top runs.
	- Notes:
		- Pre-next-cut.
		- `top` and `htop` used to smoothly animate disappearing and appearing lines. Now they don't. And even when the smooth animation worked in those programs, it would quit working after a while. It's not a high priority to get back, more of a nice-to-have.
	- Reproduced: No, not as something that fades with time. On dev, top in a window on b23 slid as often after 24 minutes as in its first minute, with its list moved by arrow keys every 20 s. Minimizing until the GPU was let go and restoring didn't stop it, and neither did wheel scrolling.
	- Possible cause: The cause is the load rather than SilkTerm. top runs on the normal screen and redraws every row each tick. Its list only shifts while some of the rows on screen are processes that didn't use any CPU in the last tick, and a change in how many did moves them up or down. Once more processes use CPU than the window has rows, every visible row is re-sorted each tick, nothing on screen moves as a block, and the redraw cuts, as it should.
		- With the load held low, then high, then low again, 24 of 43 redraws slid, then 0 of 51, then 14 of 36. A window showed the same: 32 slide steps, none, then 19.
		- On b23 now, 24 to 39 processes use CPU in a 3 s tick. In 25 minutes of top at 40 rows, every visible row was busy in all 355 timed refreshes, and none slid. A redraw after an arrow key comes after a short tick with fewer busy rows, and 573 of 898 of those slid.
	- Progress log:
		- 20261013: Question: Was b23 busy when the sliding stopped, for example a build or test run going? Does top slide again once the box is quiet? If it does, it's top re-sorting its list and the item can close as Moot. If it stays stopped on a quiet box, a window started from a terminal with `SILK_SCROLLDBG=1` prints each redraw's shift, which would show what refuses it.
		- 20261013: Today's 3 scroll changes don't affect top. It doesn't grow any history after its first clear, so the flatpak repaint check never runs for it, its first clear already snapped, and it doesn't set a mouse or focus mode, so it keeps the minimap column.
		- 20261013: Answer (JC): A new instance also isn't smooth. So it must have been a quiet box. Which I guess is OK. Even the sliding on a quiet box.
	- Verified: a slide eases the same after 14 hours of steps every 3 s as at the start.
	- Branch: topslide
	- Test case: None, since no code changed.
	- Acceptance signoff: JC, 20261013.
	- Closed: 20261013

- ✅ Text needs to be darker and thicker in light mode.
	- `Cause:` the correction made on 20260920 was a coverage exponent, and an exponent is the wrong curve rather than the wrong number. Matching what an sRGB blend of the pair would have drawn needs about 0.53 at a quarter coverage, 0.35 at a half, and 0.18 at three quarters, so no single value fits. The one that filled the stems smudged the faint edge pixels, and the one that left the edges alone left the stems pale.
	- `Fixed:` the shader is handed the text color, its background, and an amount, and bends coverage so the finished pixel comes out where an sRGB blend would have put it. It's on fork branch `text-srgb-blend-0.11.0` at 916d2c2, which took over from `coverage-gamma-0.11.0`, and that branch is left standing. `text.dark_on_light` replaces `text.dark_on_light_gamma`, and the old key is retired rather than renamed, since its number means nothing as an amount.
	- `Decision:` the setting runs to 2.0 rather than 1.0. Everything up to 1.0 is a correction and 1.0 is the whole of it. The headroom is there because how heavy text should look is partly the display and the font. At 2.0 the counters of small letters start closing up, which the config comment says.
	- `Measured:` light theme, 12 lines of text on flat paper. Ink on partly covered pixels went from 40.3% without any correction to 51.5%. An exponent alone can never bring a pixel to solid, which was the half of the complaint it couldn't fix. Dark mode is unchanged.
	- `Note:` over a wallpaper the scrim draws a pale plate at the letter's edge in light mode, and that's the scrim doing its job rather than a fault. Nothing draws there without a wallpaper, so the numbers above are the text on its own. If it still reads light, that plate is the next thing to change.
	- `Pinned by:` dcxys `only_text_darker_than_its_background_is_corrected` and dcxyt `the_pair_reaches_the_shader_as_grays_of_its_own_brightness` in text.rs, dcxyr `an_existing_config_loses_the_coverage_exponent` in config.rs, and 4 in the fork: the curve against an sRGB blend, the 2 gates, the headroom clamp, and the shader's own text against the Rust mirror of it. There were 7 mutations, each red.
	- `Left alone:` the light themes' own foregrounds. They're already near-black, and the weight was the problem.
	- Opened: 20260921-081722
	- Closed: 20260921-092439

- ✅ In light mode the same system fonts read too thin, in the terminal and in the dialogs alike, with bold terminal text the exception.
	- `Cause:` the color pipeline blends in linear light, glyph coverage included. A half covered pixel comes out near three quarters brightness whichever way round the colors are, which is a strong edge on a dark background and almost no ink on a light one. Bold escapes it because most of its pixels are fully covered.
	- `Decision:` correct the coverage rather than blend text in gamma space. A second sRGB encode inside the text pass is the thing the color pipeline contract exists to stop.
	- `Fixed:` a coverage exponent in glyphon's fragment shader, kept in the padding its params uniform already had, on fork branch `coverage-gamma-0.11.0` at 7d515a8. At 1.0 the shader takes the old path exactly. `text.dark_on_light_gamma` sets it, default 0.65, and it applies only where the text is darker than what is behind it.
	- `Measured:` under the built-in light theme, partly covered pixels went from 42.5% ink to 48.4%, and the whole block of text from 6.9% to 7.6%. The paper behind it didn't move.
	- `Note:` one pass draws the whole main window, so a light theme thickens the menu and tab labels a little too. They're on dark chrome in both modes, so that's the wrong direction, but it's a small strip and mild. design.md says why it is left there.
	- `Pinned by:` `only_text_darker_than_its_background_is_thickened` in text.rs, and 2 tests in the fork pinning the uniform's layout and the shader's own text. Both were watched red.
	- `Left alone:` the Settings dialog doesn't have a row for it. It's a config line.
	- `Note:` the exponent was replaced on 20260921 by a correction that matches an sRGB blend. See the item at the top of this section for why an exponent couldn't finish the job.
	- It's now pinned by dcxys `only_text_darker_than_its_background_is_corrected`, which came with that correction.
	- Opened: 20260920-151907
	- Closed: 20260920-160123

	- `Reproduced:` the block listed 34 of the file's 42 headings. Of the missing ones, 3 were under Architecture, and every one under Delivery was missing. Also, 2 entries had lost the parentheses from their link text.
	- `Cause:` the block is generated by the editor's TOC extension, which only runs when that editor opens the file. A heading added by any other route is never listed, and nothing complains.
	- `Fixed:` the whole block is rebuilt, by a script that reproduces the extension's own anchor rule: lowercase, keep letters, digits, spaces, hyphens, and underscores, spaces to hyphens. It keeps underscores, which the written-down rule doesn't mention. `#api-alacritty_terminal` proves it. It was verified by rebuilding the 5 TOCs that were already current and getting them back byte for byte.
	- `Fixed:` README.md was missing a heading too, from the same cause, and is rebuilt with it.
	- `Changed:` design.md's TOC no longer has blank lines between its top-level entries. It was the only one of the 7 that did, so those were hand-added, and a generated block is the documented exception to the blank-line rule anyway.
	- `Pinned by:` dcwrr `cicd/tests/toc/run.py`, which rebuilds every TOC in the tree and fails on a difference. It runs in stage 3 and takes `--fix` to write. It also refuses 2 headings that share an anchor, which no markdown linter catches. It was watched red on the real staleness and again on a heading added to FAQ.md.
	- Opened: 20260920-130105
	- Closed: 20260920-130816

- ✅ A clipboard write can leave SilkTerm owning the selection with nothing behind it.
	- x11-clipboard drops the stored text whenever another program takes the selection, without checking when that clear was generated. One left over from an earlier hand-over, arriving after the next copy, wipes the text that copy just stored.
	- SilkTerm still owns the selection at that point, so a program asking to paste doesn't get any answer at all and waits out its own timeout. It reads as every copy route failing at once.
	- `Reproduced:` 19 broken rounds out of 900 on the stock crate, against 0 out of 900 with the fix. The driver is `cicd/tests/clipboard-race/`, run by hand.
	- `Fixed:` in the fork, on `keep-value-on-clear-0.9.3` at d2cd11f9, pulled in by `[patch.crates-io]`. The `SelectionClear` arm keeps the value and cleans up only the INCR state beside it. The value is never handed out while another program owns the selection, and the next copy overwrites it.
	- `Decision:` a fork under jim-collier rather than vendoring the crate, so the patch is one branch named for the release it sits on, the same way the engine patch is kept. The branch is the published 0.9.3 plus that one change, rather than upstream's master, which has 2 unreleased changes of its own including one that alters what a failed store reports.
	- `Left alone:` asking the server who owns the selection now, which was tried first and is worse than the bug. The crate's event loop waits on `poll(fd, -1)`, so a round trip there drains the socket, leaves a pending event in x11rb's own queue with the fd no longer readable, and the thread never wakes. That version didn't reply to any requests at all.
	- `Pinned by:` `a_stale_selection_clear_does_not_wipe_a_newer_store` in the fork, watched red against the unpatched file and green with it.
	- `Note:` checked against a real build: 12 rounds of another program taking the clipboard and SilkTerm taking it straight back, with the text readable every time.
	- It was noted since 20260905 and filed 20260919.
	- The fork's test runs in the fork rather than in this pipeline.
	- Opened: 20260919-145949
	- Closed: 20260920-095505

- ✅ The About box and the notice box don't follow a change of display scale.

	- `Note:` there is no test. Laying either box out needs a real text context, and no test in the tree builds one.

	- Closed: 20260920-092436

- ✅ The Settings dialog can be left at the wrong size after a change of display scale.
	- The layout moves to the new scale, but nothing asks the window for a size to match it, so they only agree because the toolkit asks for one straight after. Where the window manager declines, such as a maximized or tiled window, the dialog draws at the new scale inside a window that kept its old size, and clicks no longer hit what they appear to.
	- The screen caps are measured again at the same time but nothing is held to them, so a window dragged from a wide screen to a smaller one at a higher scale can come out taller than the screen, with the footer buttons under the taskbar.
	- `Fixed:` the dialog is handed the size the window measures, and the window is asked for that size held to the new caps. Both halves now happen whether or not a resize follows.

	- Closed: 20260920-092436

- ✅ Selecting text all the way to the bottom of the screen - or all the way to the top - no longer auto-scrolls to reveal more to keep selecting. (It worked at some point in the past, possibly weeks ago.)
	- `Note:` this isn't a regression. The whole history was searched, and no pane ever had this. The only edge autoscroll in the tree is the Settings dialog's, for text fields.
	- `Fixed:` a drag held past the top or bottom of its pane scrolls that way and keeps selecting. A pointer outside the pane is pulled to the nearest edge cell instead of being ignored, so a drag into a neighboring pane also stays with the one it started in.
	- `Decision:` the speed is the larger of how far past the edge the pointer is and how long it has been held there. Distance alone leaves a maximized window creeping, since its top edge is already at the top of the screen. See design.md.
	- `Measured:` at 24 rows, a 3 second hold selected 133 lines dragging up and 127 dragging down.
	- `Left alone:` there's no extra CPU once the view is pinned at either end, since it stops asking for frames. That was measured against an idle control.
	- `Pinned by:` dcwgk `a_drag_past_an_edge_scrolls_and_one_inside_does_not` and dcwgm `holding_at_an_edge_with_no_room_still_builds_speed`, both mutation-checked.
	- Opened: 20260919-154614
	- Closed: 20260920-084744

- ✅ The copy-to-clipboard bug is back. First, figure out why it keeps regressing.
	- Auto-copy on select doesn't work. (With the appropriate setting enabled. Even muffer's autocopy doesn't work.)
	- CTRL+shift+C on selected text doesn't work.
	- Right-click and choose "Copy", DOES work.
	- Note: There's some chance this is a bug in muffer (whether or not autocopy is enabled), and possibly not silkterm's.
		- With muffer autocopy disabled, I can't get XFCE terminal to copy the selection. Even the Copy menu is grayed out, seemingly indicating it doesn't notice that anything selected.
		- With muffer autocopy enabled, it doesn't always work.
		- It seems the longer the muffer session, the less likely it is to work.
	- Why it keeps coming back: there are 4 ways to copy, each with its own gate, and every fix so far dealt with only one of them.
		- Right-click Copy doesn't have a gate, which is why it works.
		- Ctrl+Shift+C was dropped whenever the window-focus flag read false. That gate came in with the bare arrow fix.
		- Copy on select only runs after a drag SilkTerm saw itself. A program that tracks the mouse, like muffer, takes the drag.
		- muffer's own auto-copy asks the terminal to set the clipboard with an escape sequence, and SilkTerm has never acted on that request.
	- Changed: Ctrl+Shift+C copies even while the focus flag reads false. It doesn't type anything, so it can't be the bare arrow that gate stops.
	- Changed: a program can now set the clipboard, and on Linux the primary selection, from the pane in use. Other panes and tabs are ignored. That's the route muffer's auto-copy takes.
	- Copy on select still only follows a drag SilkTerm sees. An app that takes the mouse copies for itself now instead.
	- Interesting note: In muffer at least, if text is highlighted, then in another application text is copied and pasted, then you go back to muffer in silkterm to re-copy the still-selected text to clipboard: No mechanism will do it, not even the menu. You have to re-select the text, then it will work.
	- Cause of that last one, and it isn't one of the 4 routes: muffer tracks the mouse, so the highlight on screen is muffer's own and SilkTerm doesn't have a selection of its own to copy. The only channel is the escape sequence muffer sends when the selection is made, and it doesn't send it again afterwards. Re-selecting is what makes it send one. Nothing here can be fixed from this end without muffer offering the text again.
	- Pinned by: dd5pb `a_copy_the_user_drives_does_not_wait_on_window_focus` and dd5pc `a_program_sets_the_clipboard_only_from_the_pane_in_use`.
	- Opened: 20260909
	- Confirmed in use 20260919: the 3 changed routes work. The hotkey copies with the window out of focus, and a program setting the clipboard itself works from the pane in use.
	- Left alone: re-copying a selection an app drew itself. That's the app's highlight rather than SilkTerm's, and the app only offers the text once.
	- Closed: 20260919-182500

The watcher also fires within half a second of the console coming back, before the X server has set the mode again, so a purge after that would spoil the fresh glyphs too.

- ✅ New text added to a screen with enough room to not have to scroll up to make new space, should never "smooth-scroll DOWN" from "beneath" the content above, last-line-first. (E.g. when pasting several lines of content at once.) It should appear first-line-first. If it can all fit on the same screen without scrolling, maybe that means popping in fully-formed, all at once. That would be preferable to oddly scrolling in from beneath an invisible horizontal curtain, last-line-first. - ✅ A performance test run while the monitor is asleep can save a rating that is too low.
	- The display then shows one frame a second, so the first profile reads as hopeless and Standard terminal is saved, without any wallpaper from then on.

- ✅ Two terminals running for around 24 to 48 hours, disappeared the moment they got focus.
	- Since 20260917, 4 dogfood windows have died this way, all on builds with the idle GPU release. The 2 here closed at 10:58:11 and 10:58:19.
	- Each one first failed to get its GPU device back after an idle release (GLXBadDrawable, then GLXBadWindow). SilkTerm logged that and planned to try again on the next input.
	- winit stores the last X error in one slot, and its IME focus and unfocus calls `expect` that slot to be empty. The next focus change found the stale GLX error there and panicked.
	- So there are 2 faults. The rebuild failed every time on NVIDIA, and any stray GLX error is fatal at the next focus change.
	- Both halves were fixed 20260918. A GLX error is claimed before winit can store it, and logged as not fatal. The release now unbinds the GL context before destroying it, since otherwise the window still has its old GLX surface and NVIDIA refuses a second one.
	- A GLX error no longer takes the window down. On the NVIDIA desktop the device now comes back after an idle release, with no errors.
	- Pinned by: dcsv5 `gl_errors_are_claimed_and_others_are_not`.
	- Opened: 20260918-110145
	- Closed: 20260918-112402

The selection ran off to the end of the text under a stationary pointer, and the release left a caret instead of the whole value selected. A box narrow enough to fit its value was fine, which is why it looked intermittent.
	- Cause: a drag held past the edge of a box keeps selecting while the view crawls, and the pointer is replayed each frame to do that. It was replayed inside the box too. A click near the right edge scrolls the view to keep the caret in sight, the replay then read a later character under the same pointer, that scrolled the view further, and so on in a loop.
	- Fixed: the pointer is only replayed while it sits past the left or right edge of the box, which is the case the replay exists for.

- ✅ nano:
	- Holding the cursor down to scroll down in a long document (which makes text move up) works well. But,
	- Holding the cursor up to scroll up in a long document (which makes text move down), is jumpy. Seems to jump ~2 lines at a time.
		- 20260915-150037: Still jumpy.
		- 20260917-055036: Still jumpy.
	- Reproduced: from the trace, an up run threw the slide away and restarted it about every other step, and each restart put the view 3 or 4 lines on in one frame. A down run ran clean.
	- Cause: nano's edit window is rows 2 to 45 of 48. Whenever the line leaving it is blank, ncurses scrolls rows 2 to 46 instead, taking the blank status row along because it can. The engine's ledger took any region change as a new scroll and started over, the reveal strip did the same, and the offset was then limited to the one row the fresh strip could fill. This was confirmed from nano's own bytes. A file without blank lines didn't have any `2;46r` at all, and one with a blank line in 5 had 4 in 17 steps.
	- Why it didn't show in testing: a slow renderer takes 5 or more steps per frame, so 2 regions never met between frames. A real GPU sees one step per frame.
	- Fixed: a scroll of a region sharing rows with the one in flight continues. The ledger narrows to the rows both scrolls moved and keeps the rows that cross that edge, whether the grid dropped them or they only stopped moving. While a slide is in flight the pane takes the record with the region and direction left open instead of clearing it each frame, and the strip keeps its rows across such a step. A region sharing no rows still starts over, so stacked tmux panes stay their own item.
	- Pinned by: dcrmk `a_slide_survives_nanos_odd_region_step` in the pane and `scroll_ledger_carries_on_across_an_overlapping_region` in the engine fork, both watched failing under the old rule.
	- Note: the engine fork's test runs in the fork rather than in this pipeline.
	- It was confirmed fixed on the reporting desktop, 20260917.
	- Opened: 20260911-124508
	- Closed: 20260917-143700

- ✅ Cursor blink doesn't seem to pause after an inactivity timeout. (Only on focus lost.)
	- Reproduced: a program that moved the cursor every 2.5s kept the animation running for as long as it ran, with nothing typed. A quiet pane stopped on time, which is why this only showed with something on screen doing its own thing.
	- Cause: the stop was measured from the last time the cursor moved, rather than the last time the user did anything. A clock in a prompt, or any TUI on its own timer, resets that every few seconds. Focus loss parks by a different route, which is why that half worked.
	- Fixed: the pane remembers when it last had input or a refocus, and the long stop reads that. The resume delay after typing still reads the cursor's own stillness, which is what it is for.

- ✅ A variable in a shell's own arguments is still expanded when it is spelled the way this platform spells it.
	- Reproduced: with `bash -c 'echo $FOO'` on Linux, or `cmd /k echo %PATH%` on Windows, the program got that word already replaced. Quoting didn't protect it, and there was no way to write a literal `$` or `%`.
	- Cause: `command_argv` expanded every word of a command, rather than only the program.
	- Decision: the program name is expanded, because nothing else would. SilkTerm starts it directly. Every argument after it is passed to the program as written, on either platform.

	- Note: this also undoes the narrowing it was split from the same day. A setting that names a path reads all 3 spellings on both platforms again, which is what a config file moved between machines needs. See the Done feature "Pre-interpret the most common bash environment variables".

	- The fault is in shcl's save. When Windows has already removed the old file but can't put the new one in its place, shcl tries once more, and if that fails too it deletes the new copy as well.
	- A save from Settings, the performance rating, and 2 of the rewrites at launch all save this way. Converting an old flat file makes a backup before that save.
	- It hasn't been seen yet. It follows from shcl's code and the Windows documentation, and shcl's current code does the same.
	- The same happens with a second Windows error of this kind, which another program's settings file is known to have lost this way.

- ✅ Wallpaper disappears from the background.
	- Test case 20260910-071431: On many of (several) open silkterms that were open overnight (some for days), the wallpaper disappeared to a black background, IIRC when "enter" was pressed.
	- Wallpapers disappeared on 2 instances that had been running for ~14 hours.
	- Did NOT disappear on 3 instances of the same version, that had been running for 2 days.
	- Did NOT disappear on 1 instance of the same version, that had been running for ~19 hours.
	- New launches have no wallpaper. This may be a regression of the same bug that has been logged once or twice before.
	- This isn't a regression of the earlier wallpaper fixes. The cause was the automatic performance watch.
	- With the monitor asleep, the display driver slows a window to one frame a second. The watch took that for a slow machine and stepped down until it got to Standard terminal, which doesn't have a wallpaper. Each step was saved, so new windows started there too.
	- Fixed: a step down now lasts only until SilkTerm restarts, and never goes below Low, which still shows the wallpaper. Only frames drawn while the window has focus count, and long stalls don't count at all.
	- Automatic ratings are taken once more after updating, which undoes a step that was already saved.

- ✅ The ARM64 Windows binary has no icon and no version information, and says nothing about it.
	- Measured in the built executable: the x86_64 one had the whole version block and the copyright marker intact, and the ARM64 one didn't have any version resource at all, neither the strings nor the icon. So on that architecture Explorer showed a generic icon, the Properties tab was blank, and the installer picked up the same generic icon.
	- The missing warning was the worse half. The step is non-fatal on purpose when nothing can compile a resource for the architecture, and it is meant to say so, but neither build printed anything.
	- Cause: there were 2 faults. The resource compiler was chosen by the build machine instead of the target, so for ARM64 nothing was found. And "found nothing" was reported as "not attempted", which the caller read as success.
	- Fixed: the compiler is chosen for the target now, from a short list tried best first, and the one on this machine that can do every architecture is found even though it is only installed under a version suffix. `SILK_WINDRES` names one outright for a toolchain with some other name. A miss now warns.
	- Also fixed at the class: the pipeline reads the resource directory out of every Windows binary it built and fails if the icon or the version block is absent. A resource that silently stops being embedded isn't a link error and doesn't show up anywhere else.
	- Both Windows binaries now have the icon and version resources, and the copyright marker reads back intact from each. Forcing the compiler to fail was checked both ways. The warning appears and the pipeline check rejects the build.
	- It hasn't been verified on ARM64 Windows hardware, since there isn't any here.
	- A related fault was fixed with it. The Windows runner only reads its options before the command, so asking it to sync a branch with the option written afterwards synced the default branch instead and said nothing. Arguments a command doesn't take are now refused.
	- Pinned by: `cicd/utility/pe-resources.py --require` in the release stage, and dcrrh `cicd/tests/packaging/run.bash`.
	- Opened: 20260910-075500
	- Closed: 20260910-093000

- ✅ Windows: keystrokes injected as characters rather than keys are ignored.
	- Windows lets a program send a character directly instead of a key press, and it arrives tagged as a packet rather than as a key. Nothing types that way by hand, but the touch keyboard does for some characters, and so do text expanders and some accessibility tools.
	- An ordinary window in the same session, sent the same text the same way, receives it. The terminal receives nothing at all. Sending real key presses works fine, which is what hid this.
	- Cause: such a character arrives as a key the layout can't name, with only the text it stands for, and everything that reads a key event reads which key it was. So nothing got it. The shell, hotkeys, menus, and the Settings dialog's fields all missed it.
	- Fixed: the key is filled in from the text where the event arrives, once, so every reader of it sees the character. A key the layout did name is left alone.
	- Seen on both Windows machines with the fix in, and on one of them before and after. An injected line went nowhere on the old build and runs on the new one. An accented character and a CJK character both arrive, and ordinary typing is unaffected.
	- A couple of related faults were fixed with it. The unit suite hadn't compiled on Windows since a stray attribute left one test ungated, and 2 lint findings were in code this machine never compiles. Both are now caught here, since the lints run a second time for the Windows target, which takes under a minute and doesn't need a Windows machine.
	- The remote job runner can put a machine on a named branch, so a fix gets tried on Windows before it is merged rather than after.
	- Pinned by: dcdcy `an_unnamed_key_is_read_as_its_text`, dcdcz `a_key_with_no_text_stays_unnamed`, dcdd0 `a_key_the_layout_named_is_left_alone`, and dcdcx `cicd/tests/wingui/injchar.ps1`.
	- Opened: 20260908-141500
	- Closed: 20260909-171500

	- A Windows console names a new window after the program it starts, so a shell that doesn't set a title of its own arrives with its own image path. Confirmed for cmd and for pwsh on both test machines.
	- A console that names the program and then the command it is running keeps the command. The name has to be a full path for that, so vim's "build.bat - VIM" is left alone.
	- Seen on Linux against a live pane fed each kind: the reported title, a running command, and an ordinary title that has to survive untouched.
	- It hasn't been run on Windows, where the titles come from. An elevated pane is also unchecked. An elevated console labels its own window "Administrator: ...", and whether the terminal ever sees that is unknown, so nothing was built for it.

	- Closed: 20260909-104500

- ✅ Settings dialog: on a 1080p screen at 150% the buttons sit under the taskbar.
	- Measured on Windows: the dialog came up 831x1063 while the usable screen is 1920x1008, so the bottom 55 pixels were behind the taskbar, which is where Cancel, Apply, and OK are. There was no way to press OK.
	- Cause: the height was clamped to the monitor rather than to the part of it a window can occupy. The dialog reads the work area now, on Windows and on X11, and takes the window frame off that. A dialog centered over a tall terminal is also pulled back onto the work area rather than only off the screen origin.
	- The height was bought back by pairing 2 rows. The hardware check and its one-shot re-test share a line, and the scrim function and falloff dropdowns sit side by side under one label. It's a general mechanism. A row declared `beside` shares the line above it and takes the right half of the control column.
	- The dialog resizes now. When it's narrower than it wants, the rows scroll sideways on a bar above the footer. When it's shorter, they scroll as before. The tab strip and the buttons stay out of the vertical scroll. A resize passing within a few pixels of the natural size settles on it. The size is kept for the session and isn't written anywhere.
	- Controls in the middle of a row are variable width. Sliders, text fields, and dropdowns take whatever the width leaves, while the number field and the revert arrow keep their distance from the right edge. The style guide says so now.
	- A review of the fix found 6 more, all closed with it. A performance profile governing the first half of a shared line silenced the one revert arrow for the second half, which the profile doesn't govern and which didn't have any other way back. The tab strip was riding the sideways scroll and could pan off the window edge. It has an offset of its own now and only moves to keep the current tab in view. The snap could pull the window back to a size the screen can't fit, and it ignored the size a platform reports when it resizes on the spot. The work area was read off the dialog's own monitor rather than the terminal's, which on a second monitor is the wrong screen. And on X11 the work area spans every monitor at once, so it is now a cap rather than the size to use.

- ✅ A prompt coming back after a command slides in oddly:
	- When the screen is not full, and a command finishes, the new command prompt appears to slide down, from under the stationary contents above it. (As if sliding down from "behind" content above with a hard horizontal edge.)
	- It is more pronounced with two-line prompts (e.g. from x9ps1-git), but the same thing happens even on one-line prompts.
	- 20260905-124927: It's still present, or at least still manifests under a specific scenario:
		- When the two-line x9ps1-git prompt is in effect (e.g. cwd is a github repo).
	- First diagnosed cause (probably incorrect): the output chase was only a speed CAP on the plain navigation ease, so any advance short enough that the ease was the slower of the two got the ease instead. That ease decays on a fixed 230ms constant no setting reaches, and it hands over to the sharpened stop inside the last fraction of a line - which is where the speed picks back up. A returning prompt is one or two lines, so it hit this every time.
	- First fix (didn't work): while a burst is in flight the chase drives the view rather than capping it. Its segments already end exactly where the stop band begins, so the handover is continuous, and the 5 feel settings now govern a 2-line advance the same way they govern a long one. Measured here, a prompt arrives in about a third of a second instead of half a second, with no stall in the middle. Long bursts are unchanged.
	- It isn't a regression from the tmux work, since a build from before it shows the same stall, slightly longer.
	- Real cause: ble.sh makes room for its prompt with insert-line and delete-line on the blank rows under the cursor. Since the scroll ledger went in, the engine reports that as a region scroll. On a screen that isn't full nothing else moves, so the prompt drawn right after was eased down inside that region, while the rows above stayed still. Before the ledger, the row diff never read it as a scroll, which is why it started with the tmux work.
	- Fixed: a recorded scroll is eased only when something visible moved, a row with text on screen before it or one that left. The same redraw on a full screen with a full scrollback also lost the count of lines that went into history, so the view jumped and then slid. That count is now kept on its own through the redraw.
	- Pinned by: dc821 `a_scroll_of_blank_rows_is_not_slid` and dc822 `the_output_ease_keeps_its_count_through_a_prompt_redraw`.
	- Opened: 20260904-160838
	- Closed: 20260904-160838
	- Opened: 20260905-124907
	- Closed: 20260905-194044

- ✅ Settings refuses to open after a few times.
	- Cause: the dialogs' shared GPU context is built once on a worker thread and kept, but asking for it took the stored state unconditionally and only put it back while the worker was still running. So the second ask dropped the built context and every ask after that didn't get anything. Each open then built a whole instance, adapter, and device of its own, and those pile up until the driver refuses to allocate another swapchain.
	- Fixed. The state is put back whatever it was, so one context is used by every dialog for the life of the process. Opens after the first are also back to the speed the warm-up was meant to buy.
	- Pinned by: dc7mx `a_settled_context_survives_being_settled_again` and dc7my `a_failed_warm_up_stays_failed`.
	- Opened: 20260905-190000
	- Closed: 20260905-190000

- ✅ Wallpaper vanishes instead of falling back, and a profile round trip doesn't bring it back.
	- With the wallpaper on and no image named, the built-in shows at launch but disappears on the first settings change that touches the wallpaper.
	- Setting the performance profile to "Standard terminal" and back to "Max silk" leaves the window with no wallpaper at all.
	- Cause: both are the same thing. A rotation folder is configured or found by convention, so the built-in is suppressed, since the folder is meant to supply the picture. But only a request that reads the folder picks one, and a settings change doesn't read it. Switching the wallpaper off drops the pick, so switching it back on didn't have anything to show or to fall back on.
	- Fixed. A request reads the folder whenever there is one and nothing has been picked from it, so an empty folder falls back to the built-in and turning the wallpaper back on picks again. Rotation timing resumes with it, which it didn't before. Separately, an image that won't open now falls back to the built-in even inside a rotation folder, since a file that can't be read doesn't supply anything.
	- Pinned by: dc7k2 `a_rotation_folder_with_nothing_showing_is_read_again`, dasfm `an_unreadable_image_still_falls_back_to_the_builtin`, and dasfn `an_empty_rotation_folder_falls_back_to_the_builtin`.

- ✅ Automatic performance detection is not sensitive enough. A remote session to an older laptop with integrated graphics, over wifi, was rated "Max silk", which feels sluggish.
	- Cause: the first pick read the adapter's own description and nothing else, so anything not flatly a software renderer started at the top. An integrated chip doesn't read as slow, and neither does a remote screen, which the graphics card never draws. The step-down meant to catch it times the frames this machine draws, which over a remote session aren't the frames anybody sees.
	- Fixed. A remote session goes straight to the lowest profile without measuring, and an adapter without a card behind it to the second lowest. Everything else is measured. The window comes up whole, then a banner covers it for a few seconds while 3 profiles are timed in turn, and the first that keeps up with the display's refresh rate is saved. The window keeps drawing underneath, dimmed, and doesn't take input while the test runs.

A burst that replaced the whole screen matched nothing, and a slow stream lost about a third of its lines. The frozen bottom rows were that guess taking an unchanged content row for pinned chrome.

The first case turned out not to be broken, since wsl.exe translates a directory it inherits on its own. The second was broken, and worse than expected. /tmp, /mnt, and /opt all resolve against the current drive, so a posix path from a WSL pane passed the existing "does it exist" check and was taken as a directory on C:, which is the garbled prompt in the report.

A burst hides the extra line inside its backlog, but a settled view under a slow progress line shows it whole.

- ✅ The dreaded "Nano Bounce Bug" is back. Or I don't think ever *really* left. This will serve as the official bug report for it, but it is referenced elsewhere and I've taken multiple cracks at it - all unsuccessful and probably chasing red-herrings. It's obviously related to smooth-scrolling.
	- Steps:

		- Observe: It pops onto the screen, and "wobbles", "violently", for maybe a second or two. The wobbling is vertically up and down only.
		- Turning off smooth-scrolling, "fixes" the problem.
	- Delay this to see if other fixes, fix this.
		- Result: Other fixes have not fixed this.
	- Cause: the smooth offset is kept in 2 parts. The grid is scrolled by a whole number of lines and the renderer draws the fraction left over. The output ease was allowed to run up to 16 lines past the end of the scrollback. The alt screen doesn't have any scrollback at all, so when nano took over mid-ease the whole part sat pinned at zero while the fraction kept counting down through the leftover backlog, wrapping through a full cell once per line. Every wrap drew as a whole-cell hop. That's also why it looked random. It needs output still easing at the moment nano starts, which a long push before `git commit` gives reliably and a quiet prompt never does.
	- Fixed: the view can no longer sit past the grid. Entering the alt screen stops the ease on the spot, which is the cut a screen swap wants anyway, and a shallow scrollback caps how far a fresh terminal's first output eases. Both halves of the residual one-line scroll on alt-screen enter and exit are fixed by it too.
	- The scroll harness has a fifth scene for it. In that scene, a burst still easing when an alt screen takes over has to stay still.

Everything the user exported themselves is still inherited, which is the whole point of opening a terminal from a shell.

- ✅ Under heavy output the window burned more CPU on being told about it than on parsing and drawing it.
	- Measured on 32 MiB of output: about 20,000 "there is new output" events were sent to the window, and 2.5 seconds of the window thread went into the operating system's message queue delivering them. That was against 0.5s of parsing, 0.03s of laying out text, and 0.2s of the work the events asked for.
	- Fixed by letting one notice stand until the window takes delivery of it. Nothing is lost, since the notice doesn't have any content, so the window always reads the grid as it stands.

- ✅ Windows: output throughput is about a seventh of Linux, and a ninth of Windows Terminal on the same machine.
	- Measured 2026-08-18 on the VM at the shootout's own 160x42 grid: 12.4 MB/s of plain ASCII, against 86.9 for the same build on Linux, while Windows Terminal on that same VM reads 112.4.
	- Measured the same day, none of it is ours. A stand-in consumer that reads the bytes and throws them away, without a parser, a grid, any drawing, or an event loop, runs the real benchmark at 12.33 MB/s where the terminal itself gets 12.44, and every other width class agrees within a percent too. The limit is ConPTY, and the terminal already runs at it.
	- Nothing on our side of the pipe changes it. Microsoft's own newer console host, every pseudoconsole mode flag including passthrough, and pipe buffers from the default up to 16 MB are all inside the run-to-run noise, and the newer host is slightly slower.
	- So there isn't anything to fix in the terminal engine, and the idea of forking it for this is dropped. The freeze fix stays pinned for its own reasons.
	- Another finding is that the benchmark's barrier gets its reply from the console host on Windows rather than from the terminal, so a Windows figure times the whole chain and can never be read as one terminal's speed. Both the tool and the benchmark notes say so now, and the earlier claim to the contrary is corrected in the spreadsheet.
	- Reopened and re-measured on 2026-08-18 once a barrier-free instrument put the real end-to-end gap at about 2x rather than 10x. The same 32 MiB of output went through 4 consumers on the same box: bytes read and thrown away 1.45s, one thread reading and parsing 1.94s, the stock engine plumbing without any window at all 2.45s, and the terminal itself the same 2.5s plus its scroll ease settling. Windows Terminal is around 1.3s, which is the console host's own ceiling. It runs at that ceiling, and SilkTerm runs at about 60% of it.
	- What is left to gain is therefore about a second per 32 MiB, and none of it is in the drawing. Parsing is half a second of that, and the rest is the engine's Windows pipe plumbing, which delivers about 17 MB/s where a plain blocking read of the same pipe gets 22. A couple of obvious levers were tried, and neither changed it. They were folding the engine's internal notifications, and waiting for the pipe to accumulate before reading it. Reading and parsing on one thread beats the stock 2-thread arrangement by half a second, which is the direction to try if this is ever picked up again, and it would mean a real fork.
	- Also settled: the console host's delivery ceiling is fixed. Pipe buffers from the default to 16 MB, read sizes from 64 KB to 1 MB, and Microsoft's redistributable host beside the executable are all within noise.
	- There's no test, since it was a measurement and nothing changed.
	- Note: 20260930, the first 4 sub-bullets were the first answer. The reopen below corrects them. The gap is about 2x rather than 10x, and a single-thread read and parse is still a direction if this is picked up again.
	- Opened: 20260818-054058
	- Closed: 20260818-062827

- ✅ Windows: a long run of output freezes the window for good.
	- The window stops for good. Both ends sit idle with the writer blocked in a write that never returns, and the window doesn't use any CPU at all while stalled. It is a circular wait.
	- It's reachable by ordinary use. Anyone who cats a large file, or runs a build with a lot of output, can hang the window and have to kill it.
	- Corrected: ASCII isn't exempt. It was thought to be, but it stalls too, only later and at a point that moves between runs. Non-ASCII merely arrives sooner and stalls on the same byte every time.
	- The cause is back-pressure, whatever the content. A quarter-megabyte payload finishes, 2 megabytes stalls, and the stall point is identical whether the window is in front or behind.
	- It isn't the console. A newer bundled ConPTY still stalls, as below, and a minimal test host driving the same system ConPTY never stalls at all, even with a deliberately slowed reader.
	- Diagnosed: it is in the terminal engine we depend on. A build without a renderer, a window, or any drawing at all, only the engine's own pty and event loop, stalls at the identical byte. So nothing in SilkTerm is involved.
	- The engine reads the console into a one-megabyte staging buffer on a helper thread and tells the main loop "there is data" only as a side effect of writing into that buffer. If the main loop goes back to sleep while data is still buffered, nothing is left to tell it. Once the buffer is full there can be no further write, so the notice can never come. The reader waits for room, the main loop waits for a notice, and neither can move. That is why it needs a big burst, why it is unrelated to the console, and why both ends sit idle.
	- The fix that was found and proven is to have the reading thread announce data itself instead of relying on that side effect. The change is 2 lines. With it, payloads 4 times the size that used to hang complete normally, on the stock console.
	- Upstream hadn't fixed it, and there wasn't any issue or report. The file has had 2 commits in its life and has been wrong since the one that introduced it, in October 2023.
	- It was submitted as alacritty/alacritty#9026.
	- In the meantime, the workspace pins the released engine plus that one change, so our builds are fixed now rather than waiting. Cargo records the exact commit, so a build is still reproducible.
	- Follow-up when a release includes it: drop the pin from the workspace file, which says so in place, and delete the branch it points at.
	- There's no test here, since the fix is in the engine fork's Windows PTY code, and its tests run only there.
	- Note: 20260930, this is out of date on 2 points. The engine is kept on the fork branch `scroll-ledger-0.26.0` with several patches rather than a one-change pin, and the fix is pinned by a fork test and a SilkTerm Windows flood test, dct7y `a_pane_under_a_flood_keeps_saying_there_is_more`. alacritty/alacritty#9026 was closed unmerged, so the change stays on the fork.

- ✅ On Linux, an arrow pressed as part of a desktop-switching chord (Ctrl+Alt+Up and friends) reached the shell as a bare arrow - UAT.
	- A bare arrow arriving unasked walks the shell's history, and inside a full-screen program it moves whatever that program moves. Other terminals don't do it.
	- The window manager brackets its own hotkey with a focus change. On the way out the modifiers are zeroed, and on the way back in every key still physically held is replayed to us as a fresh press, before the modifiers are re-read. That replay was being taken as typing, so a held arrow was encoded with nothing held and sent on.
	- A replayed key is now treated as a report of what is held down, and is never sent to the shell. The same guard applies to the Settings and About windows, where a replayed Enter could have closed the dialog.
	- Keys arriving while the window doesn't have focus are also no longer typed, which closes the other way in for the same chord. A single line of code rolls that half back if it ever misfires.
	- `SILK_KEYDBG=1` prints every key event with its focus and modifier state, for the next time something like this needs settling.

Since the input is byte-identical across a failure and the success that follows it, the source can't be responsible.

	- Builds now also ask the compiler for a larger working stack. That is the compiler's own suggestion when it faults this way, and it reserves address space only, so it doesn't cost anything or change any output. It is a guess at the cause rather than a demonstrated fix, which is why the retries stand on their own.
	- Repeated faults at different points on identical input mean something varies between runs, which is either a latent defect in the optimizer or marginal hardware.
	- Memory is ruled out. It has been tested clean, and this machine encrypts memory. A single stray stored bit becomes most of a block once decrypted, so corruption at that scale would have brought the system down long before it showed up as an occasional compiler crash. That leaves a defect in the optimizer as the explanation, which is why the retry count is a setting rather than a fix. It works around something the project can't correct.

- ✅ Bug: repeated `clear; ls -lA ~/` scrolled smoothly the first time and appeared instantly every time after.
	- Cause: the smooth output scroll arms itself from how much the scrollback grew between 2 drawn frames. `clear` empties the scrollback, and re-running the same command refills it to exactly the same depth, both inside a single read of the program's output, so the measured growth was zero and nothing was armed, even though a screenful of lines had gone past. The end state doesn't have any trace of it either. The screen and the scrollback both look exactly as they did before, so the finished picture doesn't show that anything happened.
	- Fixed: the depth is now sampled once per read of the program's output rather than once per drawn frame, which is the only point where the emptying is still visible, and a drop is read for what it can only mean. The scrollback was cleared, so everything left in it arrived afterwards and is new. Repeats now scroll exactly like the first run.
	- Sampling gives up immediately rather than waiting its turn, so it can never hold up output. A skipped sample is picked up by the next one, and if every sample is skipped the previous behavior applies unchanged. Switching a full-screen program in or out, and resizing the window, both reset the measurement, since each moves the depth without anything having scrolled.
	- Note: the first run and every repeat now arm the same amount and glide through it identically, where before only the first did. Heavy output drains no slower than before.
	- Pinned by: dase9 `a_scrollback_clear_reads_as_everything_that_refilled_it` and dasea `missed_samples_are_recovered_not_lost`.

	- Cause: a smooth slide keeps the fixed parts of an application's screen still and moves only the scrolling middle, and it worked out which rows were fixed by checking which ones hadn't changed. That misses a fixed element whose text changes while it stays still. The indicator is painted over the last row of the transcript rather than below it, so that row differs on every step, the search for unchanging rows stopped short of it, and the indicator was treated as scrolling content. That's the same class of fault as the title bar that used to ghost in nano.
	- Fixed: the fixed rows are now also derived from what the detected scroll itself accounts for. A row a real scroll owns either moves cleanly or is one of the rows the step newly reveals. Anything else is fixed furniture and stays still. The 2 measures are combined by taking whichever pins more rows, so the previous behavior is a floor and no row that used to move can start behaving differently. Because the span is anchored on the rows that moved, it can only ever be widened outward, so an element stranded in the middle of the scrolling area can never hand the rows past it to the fixed set.

- ✅ Graphical emoji render as monochrome outlines instead of color.
	- This isn't a regression. No build renders these in color. The text stack has only ever read the older color-glyph table format (COLR v0), and every current color emoji font installs the newer one (COLRv1) alone. Such a glyph came back as an empty image, so an emoji cell drew blank. A later change made a blank cell retry through the generic monospace chain, which is where the monochrome outlines came from. That took the cells from empty to legible, and is why the symptom looks new.
	- Other terminals show the same fonts in color because their text rasterizer reads COLRv1.
	- Fixed: color glyphs are now painted directly. The paint graph is walked and rendered through a small 2D back end, then handed to the renderer's color atlas as a per-cell image fitted to the cell box. The back end has transforms, clip and layer stacks, solid, linear, radial, and sweep fills, and Porter-Duff and blend compositing. Chars without a color glyph are untouched and still take the monochrome fallback path.
	- `color_emoji` defaults to true, and turning it off restores the monochrome outlines.
	- Pinned by: daerd `colr_v1_emoji_rasterizes_in_color`.
	- Note: 20260930, the key is `text.color_emoji` now.

- ✅ Paste sent the clipboard bytes unchanged, which breaks a multi-line paste on Windows and leaves bracketed paste open to injection:
	- Description: there are 2 separate faults in the same place. (1) Without bracketed paste, an application can't tell a paste from typing, so a line break has to arrive as the Enter key delivers one, which is a lone CR. We sent whatever the clipboard contained, and a Windows clipboard is CRLF, so every row also had an LF and left the shell sitting on a continuation line. That is the ordinary case on Windows. (2) Inside a bracketed paste, an ESC in the text closes the bracket early, since the application is watching for `ESC[201~`, and everything after it is then read as keystrokes rather than as data, so pasted content can run a command that wasn't typed.
	- Fixed: one helper decides what goes on the wire. Unbracketed, every flavor of line break reduces to a single CR. Bracketed, the text passes through as the application asked for it except that ESC is dropped.
	- Steps to reproduce: paste several lines into a shell that hasn't enabled bracketed paste. Before the fix each line was followed by a continuation prompt.
	- Confirmed before and after with a pasted 5-line block in PowerShell 7.6: the old build ran the first line and then left a continuation prompt after every one of the rest, with the last line never running at all. The new build runs each in turn and leaves the final line on the prompt awaiting Enter, which is what it should do when the clipboard doesn't have a trailing newline. cmd.exe was correct before and is unchanged.

Once such repeated commands do reach the bottom, then everything scrolls up as expected.

			- Observe: The first time behaves as expected: the output happens quickly, then the next shell prompt appears below it almost immediately.
		- Run e.g. `ls -lA $TMP9` again (without clearing).
			- Observe: Things happen seemingly out of expected order:

That also applies to a desktop without any font setting at all, which used to claim it was following a font that didn't exist.

- ✅ Running `top` results in a scrolling bounce on each refresh.
	- It only happened once the scrollback was full, which is the steady state for a terminal that has been open a while. Past that point the line count stops growing, so the advance has to be inferred from how the on-screen rows moved.
	- `top` repaints its whole screen in place without scrolling, and almost every row changes each refresh, so no shift matched. The remaining test was whether the top line changed, and `top` keeps a clock up there, so it always had. That read as "the screen turned over in one fast burst" and reported the largest possible advance, so the view was kicked up a screenful and eased back once per refresh.
	- Inferring the advance now also requires that a line scrolled off. A repaint in place doesn't push anything into the scrollback, while a real burst pushes plenty, which separates the 2 cases at the mechanism rather than by guessing from the content. Fast output at a full scrollback still eases exactly as before.

- ✅ `--shell` eats backslashes, so a Windows path can't be passed unquoted.
	- The shell string was split with POSIX rules, where an unquoted `\` escapes the next character, so `--shell C:\windows\system32\cmd.exe` arrived as `C:windowssystem32cmd.exe` and the spawn failed with "File not found". `\\host\share` lost a leading slash the same way.
	- Outside quotes a backslash now only escapes whitespace and quotes, and is kept as-is before anything else, so plain Windows and UNC paths survive. Escaping a space or a quote still works, and inside double quotes the usual escapes are unchanged, since that path already handled Windows paths correctly.
	- The same parser reads `default_shell` and `command_line` in the config, so those are fixed too.
	- It was found while getting the Windows build to run under wine.
	- Pinned by: dact6 `shell_keeps_unquoted_backslashes` and dact7 `shell_still_escapes_whitespace_and_quotes`.
	- Opened: 20260725-161114
	- Closed: 20260725-163429

- ✅ When splitting panes, there is "visual garbage" in the pixels immediately surrounding the split lines.
	- It seems like one pixel above, below, or on (for horizontal split), or one pixel to the left, right, or on for vertical splits.
	- There were 2 causes, both fixed. The first was that the text scrim, which is the readability halo, was a full-frame blur clipped only to the whole terminal area, so an edge glyph's halo spilled across the divider into the inter-pane margins. Each pane's scrim is now clipped per side, to the content edge at internal dividers and to the pane edge at the window border, so the outer margin keeps its halo.
	- The second was the persistent sliver. A pixel-delta wheel, such as a touchpad or a hi-res wheel, accumulates fractional scroll amounts, and the ease settled wherever the target ended up, so a pane could rest between lines forever. Every row then rendered shifted by a sub-cell fraction and the top scanlines of the first clipped row peeked out at the pane's content bottom, right against the divider, on any scrolled pane, focused or not. The scroll now glides to the nearest whole line at rest.
	- Per-cell fallback glyphs were also clipped to the pane rect instead of the content rect, so an edge row's glyph could paint into the margin. They're now clipped like all other text.
	- The third cause was the one that survived the first 2 fixes. With transparency off, the 1px divider gap was still see-through, since the frame cleared fully transparent whenever the see-through-capable backend was in use, regardless of the setting, and only the wallpaper's low opacity made it to the gap pixels. The window always has an alpha channel on X11, so the compositor blended the desktop through the divider slits. Whatever was behind the window showed as bright speckles along the split lines. Only a live compositor shows it, since it is the desktop blending through. The clear is now opaque unless transparency is enabled. With it on, the gap still shows the desktop as intended.
	- Pinned by: dabej `fractional_wheel_rests_on_a_whole_line`.
	- Opened: 20260724-080316
	- Closed: 20260724-131129

- ✅ Crash: a screen filled with distinct emoji aborts the terminal.
	- Cause: color glyph images are cached per glyph and pixel size, and that cache emptied itself completely whenever it filled up. A screenful of emoji is far more distinct glyphs than it could store, so the moment it filled part-way through drawing a frame it threw away images that frame was still using, and the renderer stops dead when an image it was promised goes missing.
	- It's only reachable with a lot of different emoji on screen at once. Repeating the same few never fills the cache, which is why ordinary use never ran into it.
	- Fixed: the cache now only discards images that no recent frame has touched, and keeps far more before it tries. If everything in it is still in use it grows, which is bounded by what fits on screen.
	- Pinned by: daggh `overflow_keeps_every_raster_the_current_frame_warmed` and daggj `overflow_drops_rasters_no_recent_frame_touched`.
	- Opened: n/a
	- Closed: 20260728-074118

- ✅ Severe bug: `flatpak update` output bounces wildly.
	- It seems like every update to the update bar at the bottom, causes about a screen's worth of text to back-up a "page" (text moves down), then immediately smooth-scroll back "up", so that the bottom (update bar) is visible again. While the "Nano Bounce Bug" is just a slightly annoying but tolerable inconvenience, this one is a breaking issue.
	- But only if the text filling the terminal is from flatpak. If it's from other programs and flatpak only adds a few lines, there's no problem.
	- Cause: once a pane's scrollback is full, how far the view is behind can no longer be read from scrollback growth, so it is inferred by matching this frame's rows against the last frame's. That match demanded that nearly the whole retained region line up exactly, with at most 3 rows off. flatpak keeps a multi-row live progress area pinned at the bottom and rewrites all of it every tick, so an ordinary one-line advance always left more than 3 rows differing, no shift matched, and the inference fell through to its last-resort guess, which assumed the screen turned over completely and reported the maximum catch-up distance. Every line of output therefore kicked the view up the full backlog cap and eased it back down. That also explains why it only showed when flatpak's own output filled the screen. A few flatpak lines among other text leave the progress area too small to break the tolerance.
	- Fixed: the inference now scores every candidate shift by how much of the retained region it explains and takes the best one, instead of insisting nearly all of it lines up. The true shift always explains the most, and a coincidental match further down has less overlap to win with, so the real one-line advance is reported even while a large live region churns. The guard that a static or blank field must not read as a scroll is unchanged, and a genuine full-screen turnover still reports the catch-up distance. It's the same tolerance the alt-screen detector has used all along, since a live progress area is a static band in all but name.
	- Pinned by: dct9d `a_status_bar_is_held_still_at_a_full_scrollback_too`.
	- Opened: 20260723-135701
	- Closed: 20260723-141732

- ✅ Copy on output is still copying the prompt that appears after command output.
	- Cause: the multi-line-prompt strip matched prompt rows by exact content, so any prompt row with dynamic content, such as cwd, git branch, clock, or right-aligned segments, never matched between commands and its rows stayed in the copy.
	- Fixed: prompt rows are now matched by structure. Runs of letters and digits and of spaces collapse before hashing, so content can change while the punctuation and box-drawing layout still has to match exactly.
	- Pinned by: da8s6 `capture_strips_dynamic_prompt_rows` and da8s7 `skeleton_hash_collapses_dynamic_runs`.
